text:
The US plans to soon ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access ‌to US phone numbers on national security grounds — a measure designed to prevent scam-related robocalls.

🇺🇸 FCC said on Oct 29 that it will vote on Nov 19 on a proposal to ban China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom and other IP-enabled service providers from direct access.

For telecom firms providing VoIP — technology that converts voice into digital data and transmits it over broadband connections — direct access is ⁠a much cheaper option and makes it easier to offer advanced features.

“With this decision, the FCC will be strengthening our first line of defense against bad actors and illegal robocallers.”

The FCC also said on Oct 29 that it plans to bar IP-enabled service providers that use equipment from companies on the ‌FCC's ⁠list that pose national security risks, such as Huawei or ZTE.

The agency added that it would ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics in Dec 2028 and may also revoke direct number authorizations for Chinese companies that it deems to pose national security risks.

The FCC has previously barred China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom from providing international telecommunications services to the US.

Other measures under consideration include barring them from connecting to US networks and from operating their data centers in the US.

Concerns about the potential for spying and other harms to arise from Chinese access to US telecom data and infrastructure have grown in recent years.

In ⁠late 2024, Washington said a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group known as Salt Typhoon stole consumers' call records, US call data, and infiltrated US telecommunications and telecom infrastructure firms.

In July, the FCC added California-based Digitalsystem Technology to a list of companies posing risks to US national security, citing links to Chinese telecom firms and its ownership by a Chinese national.

text:
Zimbabwe to Host International Corrections and Prisons Association Conference in 2027

Zimbabwe is set to host the International Corrections and Prisons Association (ICPA) annual conference in October 2027, following an announcement made at this year's ICPA conference currently underway in Belfast, Northern Ireland.

Speaking at the gathering, which has drawn delegates from around the world, Commissioner General of the Zimbabwe Prisons and Correctional Service, Dr Moses Cyril Chihobvu welcomed member countries to experience Zimbabwe as they attend the association's annual conference next year. He expressed gratitude to the ICPA Board for entrusting Zimbabwe with the hosting role. "We regard this honour not only as a privilege but as an opportunity for Africa to showcase its innovations, share its experiences and contribute to the global future of corrections," Dr Chihobvu said. "Zimbabwe and other African correctional services are advancing reforms that place rehabilitation and reintegration at the heart of correctional practice. We therefore look forward to ICPA 2027 as a platform for strengthening these efforts that leave no one and no place behind he added. 

During a side meeting with the President of ICPA, Ms Heidi Washington of the United States, the Commissioner General received a warm endorsement of next year's hosting. "On behalf of ICPA, we are so excited to come to Zimbabwe in 2027 and learn about all the innovations and advancements going on in corrections there," Ms Washington said. "We will come together with our global community to share ideas and learn from one another. In addition, I look forward to seeing all the beautiful sights and scenes and everything Zimbabwe has to offer."

The Executive Secretary of ICPA, Natalia Boar of Australia, also endorsed the visit, saying it was an honour to learn about correctional practice while in Zimbabwe. She urged fellow participants to join her in the country for the 2027 conference. 

The ICPA conference is an annual event where delegates from across the globe convene to share best practices in corrections. The last meeting to be hosted in Africa was held in Namibia in 2012, and Zimbabwe's hosting of next year's edition is expected to put the country in a positive global spotlight.

text:
The Evolution of Mesa/Boogie Amplifiers, 1969-2026

Mesa/Boogie originated in California in 1969 when Randall Smith began modifying Fender Princeton amplifiers, increasing their power, gain and sustain. His experiments established Mesa Engineering and helped redefine high-performance guitar amplification.

1971-1972 - The Mark I introduced cascading tube preamp stages, generating substantial distortion and sustain at manageable volumes. Its compact cabinet, powerful output section and expanded tone controls established the foundation of the Mark series.

1978 - The Mark IIA introduced footswitchable rhythm and lead channels, allowing players to alternate between clean and overdriven sounds during performance.

1980 - The Mark IIB expanded channel switching and incorporated an effects loop, enabling external processors to operate between the preamplifier and power amplifier.

1983 - The Mark IIC refined the lead circuit and switching architecture.

1984 - The Mark IIC+ introduced further preamp refinements and became one of Mesa’s most influential amplifiers. Its cascading gain stages, tight low-frequency response and optional five-band graphic equalizer helped establish a defining high-gain sound.

1985 - The Mark III introduced three operating modes: Rhythm 1, Rhythm 2 and Lead. Its shared controls offered considerable flexibility within a compact design.

1990 - The Mark IV expanded channel independence, switching options, graphic equalization and power-amplifier flexibility.

1991 - The TriAxis programmable tube preamplifier brought digitally controlled analog circuitry, MIDI program selection and multiple preamp voices to professional rack systems.

1992 - The Dual Rectifier Solo Head established a separate Mesa high-gain architecture. Its two-channel design offered selectable tube or silicon-diode rectification, allowing different power-supply responses. The Rectifier family became closely associated with 1990s hard rock and metal.

2003 - The Lone Star emphasized clean headroom, blues-oriented overdrive, reverb and vintage-inspired response, demonstrating Mesa’s development beyond high-gain amplifiers.

2009 - The Mark V combined multiple historical Mark-series voices with three channels, selectable power settings, extensive switching and graphic EQ.

2011 - The Mini Rectifier introduced Rectifier-style amplification in a compact, lower-powered format.

2018 - The Fillmore series emphasized vintage-inspired clean and overdriven sounds with straightforward two-channel operation.

2019 - The California Tweed introduced vintage American-inspired circuitry with selectable Multi-Watt power configurations.

2021 - Gibson acquired Mesa/Boogie, bringing the California amplifier manufacturer into its portfolio.

2023 - The Mark VII introduced three channels, nine operating modes, selectable power, five-band graphic EQ, MIDI control and integrated CabClone IR speaker-cabinet simulation.

Mesa’s major technical contributions include cascading preamp gain, footswitchable channels, sophisticated effects-loop integration, post-preamp graphic equalization, Simul-Class power amplification, selectable rectification and Multi-Watt power management.

Simul-Class combines different output-tube operating arrangements within one amplifier. Selectable rectification changes power-supply behavior, while Multi-Watt systems provide alternative output-power configurations. CabClone IR extends Mesa’s development into direct recording and speaker-cabinet impulse-response processing.

Randall Smith departed Gibson/Mesa in 2024. By 2026, Mesa/Boogie remaines an established manufacturer whose Mark and Rectifier families have influenced guitar amplification for more than five decades.

text:
Something enormous was living under that sand, and it had absolutely no plan to be found.

Not hiding the way a child hides, with giggles and half a foot sticking out. Hiding the way things hide when hiding is the only reason they are still alive. Quietly. Completely. With a patience that most of us will never have for anything.

And then a human hand reached in.

I have seen a lot of ocean footage. Sharks, whales, rescues, storms, things that came up from depths nobody should have to think about. This one works differently, and it took me a while to understand why. There is no chase in it. No engineered drama. No rescue boat arriving on cue. Just a shoreline, a pair of hands, and the sudden, uncomfortable realization that the ground you are standing on might not be as empty as it looks.

Think about that for a second.

Every beach you have ever walked on was a surface. A place to put a towel. A place to lose a flip-flop. A flat, boring, reliable stretch of nothing. Now picture the same beach with a second layer, a living layer, a layer of muscle and quiet decisions running directly under your feet while you argue about where to park.

That is the world this video opens a door into.

I am not going to tell you what happens in it. I am not going to describe it, because a description would ruin the only thing it has going for it: you only get one first look.

Here is what I expect will happen when you press play. You will go quiet. Not the polite quiet of a good video. The other quiet, where you lean toward the screen without noticing, where a question forms before you can stop it. How big is that thing? Was it awake the whole time? Does it know? You will watch it again. And at some point you will ask yourself a question I am still turning over, and I will get to it before this post is over.

But first, I want to talk about the strangest part of the whole thing, which is not the creature.

It is the fact that you are surprised at all.

You live on a planet where more than seventy percent of the surface is ocean. By most estimates from ocean science agencies, the large majority of that ocean has never been mapped in detail, never been seen by human eyes, never been visited by anything with a camera. We have better maps of the surface of Mars than of our own seafloor. That is not a poetic exaggeration. It is a plain fact about how little attention we have paid to the largest living space on Earth.

And yet here you are, genuinely startled that something big can live where you assumed there was only sand.

That gap, between what we assume and what is actually down there, is where this entire video lives. Every second of it sits inside that gap. And once you notice the gap, you start seeing it everywhere. In the tide pool you walked past. In the rock you stepped over. In the patch of shoreline that looked, for all the world, like nothing.

I want to walk you through why that matters, why this particular moment hit so hard, and why I think the reaction to it says more about us than about the animal. It is a long post. Stay with me. I promise the length is earned, and I promise I will not spoil the thing you actually came here for.

Because the question at the center of this video is not "what is it?"

The question is "what do we do when we find something that did not want to be found?"

THE ECONOMY OF HIDING

Start with a simple rule of the sea: almost everything in it is food for something else.

That single rule has shaped more of the living world than any other force. It explains the stripes, the spines, the glow, the ink, the venom, the mimicry. It explains why a flatfish spends its life as a pancake the color of the bottom. It explains why razor clams drop through the sand faster than a hand can follow, why sand eels vanish in a flicker, why rays settle into the seabed and leave only two eyes watching. It explains why cuttlefish can bury themselves and change their skin until even the sand seems to forget they exist.

In the ocean, being seen is expensive. Being buried is cheap.

So the sea floor is not empty. It is full of things that learned to pay the cheapest price available: stillness. A whole population of animals whose survival strategy is to become, for hours at a time, a piece of the landscape. They do not run. They do not fight. They disappear, and they trust the disappearance to hold.

Which is a remarkable kind of faith, when you think about it.

Imagine betting your entire life on the assumption that nothing will look closely enough. Every tide. Every day. Every time something passes overhead. The bet is not a dramatic one. It is quiet and constant and exhausting, and it works almost every time. That is why the animals that make it are still here.

Almost every time.

What strikes me about the footage you are about to see is that the usual predators never come into it. No jaws. No beak. No hunter built by evolution for this exact job. The thing that breaks the disguise is something the disguise was never designed to defeat. A different kind of attention. A deliberate, reaching, mammalian kind.

Camouflage is a language. It is written for a specific reader, usually a predator with specific eyes. Fish see color differently than we do. Birds see ultraviolet. Some hunters track by smell, some by vibration, some by the tiny electrical fields that living muscle gives off. Every disguise in the sea is tuned to fool a particular audience.

A human who knows where to look is a reader the language was never written for.

Think about what that means. For millions of years, an animal can perfect a trick. It gets better and better. Generation after generation, the trick sharpens, until it is nearly flawless against everything that has ever hunted it. And then one species shows up with a different kind of knowledge, a different kind of patience, a different kind of curiosity, and the entire system of protection is just a puzzle to be solved.

I do not say that to make anyone feel guilty. People have been reading the shoreline for as long as there have been people on shorelines. Coastal communities around the world have lived beside the tide for generations, and they know things about sand and water and the creatures that hide in them that no textbook fully captures. That knowledge is real, it is old, and it deserves respect.

But there is a difference between knowing the sea and getting used to it.

When something is familiar to you, you stop seeing how strange it is. The people who handle the sea every day know that better than anyone. The rest of us, watching from a distance with a phone in our hands, get the full jolt. We see it with fresh eyes, and it is a lot.

And that jolt is the second thing I want you to notice. Not the animal. The jolt.

Because the jolt is information.

It tells you how thin your mental model of the world really is. It tells you that somewhere in your head there is a picture of the ocean made of fish shapes and blue water and a few famous monsters, and that picture is wrong in ways you cannot even list. It tells you that "nothing there" is not a fact about the beach. It is a fact about your eyes.

I find that unbearably interesting. I hope you do too.

A BODY WITH NO RULES

Now let me talk about the kind of animal this might be, because it matters for the question I promised you.

I cannot tell you for certain what species you are about to watch. I will not pretend to. What I can tell you is that the sea has a whole family of soft-bodied animals, the cephalopods, that includes octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, and that if you spend an hour reading about them you will start to feel that evolution ran a second, parallel experiment in intelligence and nobody told us.

Octopuses have three hearts. Their blood is blue, built around copper instead of iron. A large share of their neurons sits not in a central brain but spread through their arms, which means that an arm can, in a meaningful sense, make decisions of its own. They can squeeze through any gap larger than their beak. They can change the color and texture of their skin in a fraction of a second. Many of them live only a year or two, some a few years more, and in that short time they learn, solve problems, escape from tanks, and remember.

Real ones. That look back.

THE LONGEST SECOND

I want to describe that moment without touching the content, because I think it is the real reason this clip travels.

It is the moment where you realize the situation is not going to resolve itself in the way you expected.

Most animal videos make a promise in the first beat. You know the genre. A creature is in trouble, a person arrives, music tells you everything will be fine. The structure is so familiar that you can relax into it, like a song you know the end of. There is nothing wrong with that. Those videos are comforting, and comfort is a legitimate thing to want from the internet.

This is not one of those videos.

This one makes a quieter promise. It leaves room to wonder, and it leaves that room open longer than most clips dare. It does not explain itself. It trusts you to sit with not knowing, and in a feed built entirely around instant reward, that is almost unheard of.

I think that is why people keep rewatching it. Not because they missed something. Because the not-knowing is the experience.

The gap is not pleasant, but it is motivating, and it gets stronger when you are close to the answer. You do not itch about things you know nothing about. You itch about things you are nearly able to see.

Good stories exploit that gap. Great stories refuse to close it too fast.

And here is the part that keeps me up: the gap here is not manufactured. Nobody wrote it into a script. It is built into the situation itself, because the situation is genuinely ambiguous. The longer you watch, the less certain you become about who is the protagonist, what the stakes are, and what the best possible ending would even look like.

Try this experiment. Before you play it, decide what outcome you want. Write it down if you like. Then watch, and see whether your answer survives the last frame.

Maybe it will. Maybe the version of you who pressed play and the version who reaches the end will not quite agree, and you will spend a while working out which one was right.

There is a lesson in there about snap judgments. About how quickly we decide that something is good or bad, kind or cruel, necessary or pointless, and how often the decision is made before the evidence is in. I think we all know that. I think we all forget it every time a short video gives us a reason to feel certain.

So go in uncertain. It is the only honest way to watch.

WHOSE BEACH IS IT

Let me move to the question that splits every comment section this kind of video lands in.

What are we allowed to do to a wild animal?

Not what is legal. That depends on where you stand, which species it is, which season it is, and which set of local rules applies, and I cannot tell you any of that from a clip. I mean the other question. The one underneath. The one most people feel before they can put it into words.

There are at least four honest answers, and every one of them has smart, decent people behind it.

The first answer is that nature is not ours to touch. Leave it alone. The best thing a human can do for a wild animal is to stay out of its life. Every handling, every disturbance, every well-meaning intervention costs the animal something, even when it looks harmless. People who hold this view are not being cold. They have usually watched what happens when attention becomes a habit, when curiosity turns into crowds, when a quiet shoreline becomes a destination. They have seen the cost, and they want it stopped.

The second answer is that humans are part of nature, and always have been. People have lived off the sea since before there were words for it. Telling them to stay away from the water because of how it looks on a phone in a city is a strange kind of arrogance. People who hold this view point out, fairly, that the most destructive relationships with the sea are rarely the small, local, hand-scale ones.

A hand to study is not a hand to sell. A hand to look closer is not a hand to prove a point to a camera. The act can be identical. The meaning is not.

I am drawn to the fourth answer. But I do not think it lets us off the hook, because the video does not let us off the hook. It puts the question in front of you with no commentary, no caption, and no verdict, and then it ends, and you are the one left standing there.

And the weirdest thing is what happens next. You start to look at your own relationship with the sea.

The seafood on your plate. The beach holiday you took last summer. The documentary about oceans that you watched with a mix of awe and guilt. The plastic in the water that you read about and then scrolled past. The way you speak about "nature" as if it were a separate place you visit instead of the system you are already inside.

None of that is on screen. All of it arrives anyway.

That is what the best videos do. They are not about what they show. They are about what they wake up.

I will tell you the thing I noticed in myself, because it is uncomfortable and I think it is common. I wanted someone to be the villain. It would have been easier. A clean moral shape, a clear side to be on, and then I could go back to scrolling with my conscience intact.

The footage does not give me that. It gives me a person and an animal and a stretch of shore. Everything else is mine to supply, and what I supply says a lot about me.

Maybe it will say something about you, too.

THE PHONE IN THE MIDDLE

There is a third presence in this video that nobody mentions, and it might be the most important one.

The camera.

Think about what it means that this moment exists as a video at all. Somebody decided to record it. Somebody kept the lens steady while something unusual was happening in front of them. Somebody judged, in real time, that this was worth keeping. Hundreds of millions of people are now able to watch an event that, in any earlier century, would have been seen by a handful of people on a shoreline and then turned into a story told over dinner.

It is what happens when a true experience has to be carried in memory.

But it comes with a cost, and the cost is attention.

Once an event is recorded, it is also performed, whether or not anyone intended it. The person in front of the lens knows, at some level, that they are being watched, and the knowledge changes behavior, even slightly. The animal, of course, has no idea. It is the only participant in the scene who is not performing. Whatever it does, it does for itself.

That is a strange thing to hold in your mind while you watch. One side of the encounter is aware of the audience. The other is aware only of the moment.

I find it oddly moving. It is one of the few places in modern life where something genuine is still happening in front of a lens, because one of the parties cannot fake it.

And then there is you.

You, with your thumb on the glass. You, in a waiting room or on a train or in bed at midnight, choosing whether to spend ninety seconds of your life on a stranger's afternoon at the water. You are also part of the scene. You are the reason it was posted, the reason it keeps spreading, the reason people will keep recording moments like it.

That is not a reason to feel bad. It is a reason to be curious about what you are doing when you watch.

Because attention is not neutral. It rewards things. A clip that gets millions of views teaches thousands of people that this is what the internet wants, and some of them will go looking for their own version. I do not know whether that is mostly good or mostly bad. I suspect it is both, in proportions that change depending on the clip and the person.

What I do know is that the healthiest way to watch is with your eyes open. To enjoy it, to feel it, and to remember that somewhere in the chain between the beach and your screen there are choices, and that some of those choices are yours.

You do not have to resolve all of that in one sitting. Just let it ride along with the video.

It is surprising how much heavier a short clip gets when you carry it that way.

WHAT THE TIDE KNOWS

One more angle, and then I will let you go.

Time.

Most of the coast on this planet is rewritten twice a day. The water comes in, the water goes out, and the sand is shuffled like a deck of cards. Whatever was hidden an hour ago is covered. Whatever was covered is exposed. The shoreline is less a place than a process, a slow, rhythmic argument between land and sea that has been running since before either had a name.

They run on a clock that has nothing to do with ours, and they have been running on it for longer than people have kept time.

So when you see a living thing wedged into that moving line, you are not looking at a random accident. You are looking at a decision made by a body that has spent its whole life studying the same few meters of seabed. A decision about where to be, and for how long, and what risk was worth taking.

And the decision was good. That is the point. The place was well chosen. The hiding was well done. By every standard the animal had ever been tested against, the plan was working.

It just had not been tested against this.

I keep coming back to that. We tend to imagine that wild animals are either lucky or doomed, that they live in a world of constant danger and constant narrow escapes. The truth is more interesting and more subtle. Most of the time, they are extremely competent. They know their world in a way that would humble any of us. And then, sometimes, the world sends something they have no category for.

What does a mind do with something it has no category for?

I do not know. Nobody does, not really. But I think it is one of the most honest questions the ocean can ask, and I think this clip asks it better than a hundred documentaries.

Which brings me back to the question I promised you earlier.

Here it is. When you finish watching, ask yourself this: if you were the one with the power, and you had no one to answer to and no one to impress, what would you want to be true about the way you used it?

Not what you would do. What you would want to be true about it.

I have tried to answer that honestly a dozen times. I get a different answer depending on the day.

Some clips get shared because they are cute. Some because they are outrageous. A rare few get shared because they hand the viewer a question they cannot carry alone.

I think this is one of those.

And the thinking is half the value. Two people watching the same handful of seconds will notice different things, argue about different details, and arrive at different feelings. One will see a skill. One will see an intrusion. One will see a wonder. None of them will be wrong, and all of them will be telling you who they are.

That, in the end, is why I wrote this much about so little.

Because the video is short, but the space around it is enormous, and that space is where the real conversation happens. It is the place where an ordinary afternoon on an ordinary shore becomes a mirror.

There is also something almost old-fashioned about it. No filter, no narration, no tidy moral stitched on at the end. Just a moment from the edge of the water, handed to you whole, with the understanding that you are an adult and can work out what you think. That kind of trust is rare online. When a clip offers it, people tend to repay it with attention, and with the kind of honesty they rarely bring to a feed.

And if you are the kind of person who keeps looking at the ocean long after the video ends, who wonders what else is down there, what else is waiting under a surface that looks like nothing, then you already understand why I could not leave this one alone. Some questions are worth being haunted by, and this is one of them.

So here is where I leave you.

You have a clip in front of you, and it is short. You will be done with it before your coffee cools. But I do not think you will be done with it that quickly. Some videos are entertainment and some are weather. You watch them, and then something in the room is slightly different.

I will not tell you how it ends. I will not tell you whether to feel relieved, or worried, or both, or neither. That is yours.

I will only tell you what I told myself after the first viewing, which I have not been able to shake.

Somewhere right now, under a stretch of ordinary sand, something is holding perfectly still and trusting that nobody is looking.

Go and look again.

Then tell me honestly what you saw.

It is what happens when a true experience has to be carried in memory.

The camera removes that. It fixes the event in place. It says: this is how big it was, this is how long it took, this is what the hands looked like. It replaces legend with evidence, and that is a gift.

But it comes with a cost, and the cost is attention.

Once an event is recorded, it is also performed, whether or not anyone intended it. The person in front of the lens knows, at some level, that they are being watched, and the knowledge changes behavior, even slightly. The animal, of course, has no idea. It is the only participant in the scene who is not performing. Whatever it does, it does for itself.

That is a strange thing to hold in your mind while you watch. One side of the encounter is aware of the audience. The other is aware only of the moment.

I find it oddly moving. It is one of the few places in modern life where something genuine is still happening in front of a lens, because one of the parties cannot fake it.

And then there is you.

You, with your thumb on the glass. You, in a waiting room or on a train or in bed at midnight, choosing whether to spend ninety seconds of your life on a stranger's afternoon at the water. You are also part of the scene. You are the reason it was posted, the reason it keeps spreading, the reason people will keep recording moments like it.

That is not a reason to feel bad. It is a reason to be curious about what you are doing when you watch.

Because attention is not neutral. It rewards things. A clip that gets millions of views teaches thousands of people that this is what the internet wants, and some of them will go looking for their own version. I do not know whether that is mostly good or mostly bad. I suspect it is both, in proportions that change depending on the clip and the person.

What I do know is that the healthiest way to watch is with your eyes open. To enjoy it, to feel it, and to remember that somewhere in the chain between the beach and your screen there are choices, and that some of those choices are yours.

You do not have to resolve all of that in one sitting. Just let it ride along with the video.

It is surprising how much heavier a short clip gets when you carry it that way.

WHAT THE TIDE KNOWS

One more angle, and then I will let you go.

Time.

Most of the coast on this planet is rewritten twice a day. The water comes in, the water goes out, and the sand is shuffled like a deck of cards. Whatever was hidden an hour ago is covered. Whatever was covered is exposed. The shoreline is less a place than a process, a slow, rhythmic argument between land and sea that has been running since before either had a name.

Animals that live in that zone have to read the argument. They know when the water will leave, when it will return, how long they have before the sun gets too hot or the birds get too close. They run on a clock that has nothing to do with ours, and they have been running on it for longer than people have kept time.

So when you see a living thing wedged into that moving line, you are not looking at a random accident. You are looking at a decision made by a body that has spent its whole life studying the same few meters of seabed. A decision about where to be, and for how long, and what risk was worth taking.

And the decision was good. That is the point. The place was well chosen. The hiding was well done. By every standard the animal had ever been tested against, the plan was working.

It just had not been tested against this.

I keep coming back to that. We tend to imagine that wild animals are either lucky or doomed, that they live in a world of constant danger and constant narrow escapes. The truth is more interesting and more subtle. Most of the time, they are extremely competent. They know their world in a way that would humble any of us. And then, sometimes, the world sends something they have no category for.

What does a mind do with something it has no category for?

I do not know. Nobody does, not really. But I think it is one of the most honest questions the ocean can ask, and I think this clip asks it better than a hundred documentaries.

Which brings me back to the question I promised you earlier.

Here it is. When you finish watching, ask yourself this: if you were the one with the power, and you had no one to answer to and no one to impress, what would you want to be true about the way you used it?

Not what you would do. What you would want to be true about it.

I have tried to answer that honestly a dozen times. I get a different answer depending on the day.

WHY THIS ONE TRAVELS

Some clips get shared because they are cute. Some because they are outrageous. A rare few get shared because they hand the viewer a question they cannot carry alone.

I think this is one of those.

You will not send it to a friend with a caption that says "look at this." You will send it with something more like "tell me what you think this is," or "am I the only one who felt weird?" That is a different kind of sharing. It is not broadcast. It is an invitation to think together.

And the thinking is half the value. Two people watching the same handful of seconds will notice different things, argue about different details, and arrive at different feelings. One will see a skill. One will see an intrusion. One will see a wonder. None of them will be wrong, and all of them will be telling you who they are.

That, in the end, is why I wrote this much about so little.

Because the video is short, but the space around it is enormous, and that space is where the real conversation happens. It is the place where an ordinary afternoon on an ordinary shore becomes a mirror.

There is also something almost old-fashioned about it. No filter, no narration, no tidy moral stitched on at the end. Just a moment from the edge of the water, handed to you whole, with the understanding that you are an adult and can work out what you think. That kind of trust is rare online. When a clip offers it, people tend to repay it with attention, and with the kind of honesty they rarely bring to a feed.

And if you are the kind of person who keeps looking at the ocean long after the video ends, who wonders what else is down there, what else is waiting under a surface that looks like nothing, then you already understand why I could not leave this one alone. Some questions are worth being haunted by, and this is one of them.

So here is where I leave you.

You have a clip in front of you, and it is short. You will be done with it before your coffee cools. But I do not think you will be done with it that quickly. Some videos are entertainment and some are weather. You watch them, and then something in the room is slightly different.

I will not tell you how it ends. I will not tell you whether to feel relieved, or worried, or both, or neither. That is yours.

I will only tell you what I told myself after the first viewing, which I have not been able to shake.

Somewhere right now, under a stretch of ordinary sand, something is holding perfectly still and trusting that nobody is looking.

Go and look again.

Then tell me honestly what you saw.

text:
The Evolution of High-Gain Guitar Amplifiers, 1959-2026

High-gain amplification evolved from amplifiers driven into distortion at high volume to purpose-built circuits producing extensive sustain, compression and harmonic complexity at controllable levels.

1959 - Fender’s 5F6-A Bassman established an influential foundation. Its 6L6 power section, phase inverter and preamp could produce substantial overdrive when pushed. It was not a dedicated high-gain design.

1962 - Marshall introduced the JTM45, adapting elements of the Bassman circuit. Subsequent Super Lead amplifiers established the powerful, non-master-volume overdrive associated with British hard rock.

1969 - Randall Smith began modifying Fender Princeton amplifiers, installing higher-powered circuitry and larger speakers. These early Boogies preceded his cascading-gain breakthrough.

1971-1972 - Mesa/Boogie’s Mark I introduced cascading tube preamp gain stages, generating substantial distortion and sustain before the power section. Multiple gain controls allowed greater separation of distortion and output volume.

1975 - Marshall’s JMP 2203 Master Volume combined cascaded preamp stages with separate preamp and master-volume controls. The 50-watt 2204 followed, extending the approach.

1981 - The JCM800 series incorporated Marshall’s established Master Volume architecture. The 2203 became a major reference for hard rock and heavy metal. Channel-switching JCM800 models followed.

1984 - Mesa’s Mark IIC+ refined high-gain lead circuitry. Optional five-band graphic equalization allowed substantial control over midrange and bass response, particularly important for tightly articulated distortion.

1987 - Mike Soldano introduced the SLO-100, employing multiple cascaded gain stages, separate Normal and Overdrive channels and a 100-watt power section. Its preamp architecture influenced later high-gain designs.

1992 - Peavey’s Eddie Van Halen-associated 5150 introduced a 120-watt, 6L6-powered platform with extensive preamp saturation. Mesa’s Dual Rectifier offered a different architecture, including selectable tube or silicon-diode rectification.

1994 - Diezel’s VH4 established a sophisticated four-channel format, providing independent gain structures and extensive switching flexibility.

2007 - The EVH 5150III expanded the 5150 lineage into a three-channel amplifier with separate clean, crunch and lead capabilities.

2019 - Friedman’s BE-100 Deluxe extended the modified-Marshall tradition through additional channel and voicing options.

2020s - Modern high-gain amplification combines refined analog gain circuits with increasingly sophisticated switching, MIDI, reactive-load outputs, cabinet impulse responses and direct recording.

The essential development was not simply more distortion. It was greater control over where distortion occurs, how its frequency content is shaped, and how the amplifier responds to the player’s technique.

text:
David Gilmour's 1994 Pink Floyd Tour Rig - How He Achieved His Sound

During Pink Floyd's 1994 Division Bell tour, David Gilmour employed one of rock's most elaborate guitar systems. Designed around Pete Cornish's custom routing equipment, the rig combined analog compression, overdrive, fuzz, modulation, digital processing and multiple tube amplifiers.

Guitars and pickups

His principal instrument was a Candy Apple Red 1983 Fender '57 Reissue Stratocaster equipped with three active EMG SA pickups, an EXG treble/bass expander and an SPC midrange control. The EMGs offered low-noise operation and onboard tone shaping. The SPC provided additional midrange emphasis for sustained lead passages.

Other instruments included Fender Telecasters, Gibson acoustics and lap steel guitars.

Compression and sustain

Three compressors were available: Boss CS-2, MXR Dyna Comp and Ibanez CP-9. Compression controlled dynamic peaks and extended note decay.

His gain devices included two Chandler Tube Drivers, a ProCo RAT, Sovtek Big Muff, Pete Cornish P-2 and Soft Sustain-2. The Tube Drivers provided boost and overdrive, the Big Muff produced sustained fuzz, and the RAT supplied an alternative distortion character.

Amplification

An Alembic F-2B tube preamplifier was part of the system, alongside modified Hiwatt DR103 100-watt amplifiers. Their substantial clean headroom preserved note definition even at concert volume.

WEM Super Starfinder cabinets with Fane speakers and Marshall cabinets provided different speaker responses. Separate amplification paths contributed to the expansive live sound. Doppola rotating speakers supplied physical modulation and movement.

Modulation, delay and spatial effects

Two Boss CE-2 chorus pedals, an Electro-Harmonix Electric Mistress flanger, rack-mounted Uni-Vibe and Demeter Tremulator supplied chorus, flanging, vibrato and tremolo.

A TC Electronic 2290, Lexicon PCM 70 and MXR Digital Delay System II provided delays and additional processing. Carefully controlled repeats extended melodic phrases without overwhelming the original notes.

The Dynacord CLS-222 simulated Leslie-style rotating-speaker modulation, complementing the Doppola cabinets.

Switching and signal integrity

Cornish's 24-loop routing system allowed effects to be selected in different combinations rather than operating as one permanently connected chain. A Bob Bradshaw programmable floor controller recalled settings for individual songs.

Impedance matching, signal levels, buffering, power distribution and noise control helped maintain clarity through the extensive equipment system.

The playing technique

Gilmour's recognizable sound depended equally on his phrasing: controlled bends, expressive vibrato, precise picking, volume manipulation and deliberate spaces between notes.

Sustain came from the interaction of technique, compression, gain, amplification and controlled feedback. His signature spaciousness resulted from balancing the direct guitar signal against carefully selected delays, chorus and rotating-speaker effects.

The defining principle was not using every effect simultaneously.

That’s completely false. Capitalist economies offer significant opportunities for social mobility, including the possibility of moving from extreme poverty to extraordinary wealth.

Consider three real examples:

Oprah Winfrey: Born into severe poverty in rural Mississippi, she became a billionaire through her career in media and business.

John Paul DeJoria: He was homeless, lived out of his car, and started Paul Mitchell with just $700. He eventually became a billionaire.

Jan Koum: He immigrated from Ukraine, relied on food stamps, and later co-founded WhatsApp, becoming a billionaire when the company was sold to Facebook.

These aren’t fictional stories. They’re real people who went from poverty to enormous wealth.

Capitalism doesn’t guarantee success, but it doesn’t condemn you to remain in the economic class you were born into, either.

text:
So I hired an attorney.

Not a friend-of-a-friend who handled wills and traffic tickets. I hired the best personal injury lawyer in Pittsburgh I could find, a woman named Marjorie Kline who wore navy suits, red reading glasses, and the expression of someone who had watched liars underestimate her for thirty years.

She came to our house because Emma still tired easily.

Marjorie sat at our kitchen table with medical records spread in front of her. She reviewed the hospital bills, surgical notes, physical therapy plan, psychological therapy recommendation, photographs of the injuries, witness names from the party, and the few text messages where Vanessa tried to frame Emma as the aggressor.

When she finished, she removed her glasses.

“This is not negligence,” she said. “This is intentional violence.”

Hearing someone say it so plainly loosened something in me.

“We can sue?” Derek asked.

“Oh, we can sue.”

We filed for assault, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, medical expenses, future care, pain and suffering, and punitive damages.

Vanessa’s attorney responded by claiming self-defense.

I laughed when Marjorie read it aloud.

Then I stopped laughing because the defense required them to call Emma dangerous.

A fourteen-year-old girl who weighed ninety pounds before surgery. A child who had been standing beside her own bike in her own yard.

Depositions began in late summer.

Vanessa sat across from me in a conference room with beige walls and stale coffee, wearing a black blazer and no jewelry. She looked thinner. Her hair was pulled back severely. If she hoped that made her look remorseful, it failed.

She looked angry.

Her attorney asked questions designed to make the party sound chaotic, the bike dispute mutual, Emma emotional.

Then Marjorie began.

“Mrs. Carter, did you strike Emma Morgan with an aluminum baseball bat?”

Vanessa’s jaw worked. “I reacted to protect my daughter.”

“Did Emma touch Brooklyn?”

“She grabbed the handlebars.”

“Did she strike Brooklyn?”

“No.”

“Kick her?”

“No.”

“Threaten her?”

“She was aggressive.”

“In what way?”

“She was yelling.”

“She said Brooklyn could not ride her bike?”

Vanessa’s eyes flicked to me.

“Yes.”

“And for that, you struck her hard enough to fracture three ribs?”

Vanessa’s attorney objected.

Marjorie waited.

I watched my sister’s face.

Not once did she look sorry.

Emma’s deposition happened two weeks later.

She wore a blue cardigan and kept one hand near her side even though the worst pain had eased. Marjorie sat beside her. I sat behind her, where she could see me if she turned.

The defense attorney tried to be gentle at first.

Then he suggested she had frightened Brooklyn.

Emma’s eyes filled, but her voice stayed clear.

“I told her not to ride my bike.”

He asked whether she had run toward Brooklyn.

“Yes. Because she was taking my bike.”

“Were you angry?”

“Yes.”

“Could your aunt have thought Brooklyn was in danger?”

Emma looked confused then, genuinely.

“No. Brooklyn was sitting on my bike. I was standing next to it. Aunt Vanessa hit me.”

The attorney tried again.

Emma started crying.

Marjorie ended it.

That night, Emma asked if telling the truth always felt that terrible.

“Sometimes,” I said. “But lies feel worse later.”

Settlement offers began after that.

The first was twenty thousand dollars.

Marjorie snorted. “Absolutely not.”

Our demand was four hundred thousand.

Medical costs. Future therapy. Pain and suffering. Punitive damages.

Vanessa would have to drain retirement accounts, sell assets, maybe her house. My mother called it financial murder.

I called it math.

Three days before civil trial, Vanessa’s side requested a meeting.

They offered three hundred twenty-five thousand dollars.

Guaranteed.

Enough to pay Emma’s medical bills, fund therapy, and secure a large portion of her college future.

Marjorie recommended accepting.

text:
Two women borrowed ₦400,000 each. Three weeks later, one was coping. The other was selling at a loss to meet the same deadline.

This fictional scene at Lagos' Mile 12 Market captures what struck me about @2FactorFinance's Live on Base announcement: matching financing terms don't create matching risks.

2Factor's public beta is live on Base, starting with cbBTC. Its Kelly-optimized leverage begins with the asset, not a standard 3x multiplier.

Holding leverage over time means facing two separate costs:
• Volatility drag: price swings can erode compounding.
• Financing drag: maintaining extra exposure costs money.

Kelly sizing accounts for an asset's long-run drift and volatility, rather than forcing one multiple onto everything. For cbBTC, 2Factor targets about 1.33x. Lower-volatility assets can support different multiples, depending on the assumptions.

It also splits exposure into two perpetual tranches:
• Senior: buffered from initial losses by junior capital, with compensation paid by the leveraged side.
• Junior: amplified exposure without conventional margin liquidation or an external hedging counterparty.

The junior can lose its entire value. Senior protection isn't unlimited.

Now picture Mile 12.

My aunt sold bags of rice. Her neighbour, Mama Bose, sold fresh pepper. Both borrowed ₦400,000 from a market cooperative to increase their stock.

Same weekly charges. Same repayment deadline.

One Wednesday, trucks arrived loaded with pepper. Supply jumped, prices dropped, and Mama Bose had barely sold half her stock. Fresh pepper doesn't wait for a better week.

My aunt was managing her payments. Mama Bose was selling at a loss to keep up.

The repayment date stayed put. The pepper price didn't.

Cooperative loans aren't leveraged tokens. But the comparison makes one point: identical financing can't cancel out differences in the asset underneath.

2Factor is working with Coinbase to extend this idea to its tokenized stocks ecosystem on Base. Tokenization puts assets onchain; this adds a way to structure exposure around their risks. Bitcoin is the live starting point; tokenized equities are still planned.

I joined Season One of the 2Factor Points Program. Verified social, educational and referral actions earn Marks. Buying, depositing or holding assets doesn't. The leaderboard freezes at launch, and the top 10 share 1 BTC in cbBTC. Marks have no cash value, cannot be transferred and give no claim on assets.

My referral link (I may earn Marks): https://t.co/kVwv8IpL5i

Would you have offered both women identical financing terms? What's the first variable you'd check before saying yes?

A Beginners Guide To Eating Oysters Elevating Your Seafood Palette

National Oyster Month is the perfect occasion to step out of your culinary comfort zone and discover one of the Gulf Coast's most celebrated delicacies. Along the coastal waters of Alabama, Florida, and Mississippi, oysters are far more than seafood—they are a cornerstone of regional maritime heritage, coastal ecology, and community life. If you have never tried an oyster before, there is no better time or place to take your first bite than during this month-long celebration.

Gulf Coast oysters are renowned for their plump, hearty size and rich, creamy flavor profile. Thanks to a thriving blend of traditional harvesting and innovative off-bottom aquaculture from local farms like Murder Point and Navy Cove, local waters yield consistently fresh, top-tier oysters often affectionately called "butter babies" by chefs and farmers. Beyond their culinary fame, oysters act as vital water filters and reef builders, making every shell an environmental ally in local estuaries.

RELATED ARTICLE:  Oysters Worth Killing For

Many newcomers assume eating oysters means swallowing a raw mollusk whole. In reality, Gulf Coast seafood houses and oyster bars offer an astonishing variety of cooked preparations and flavorful toppings designed to satisfy every palate:

Chargrilled with Garlic Butter & Cheese: The most popular entry point for beginners. Oysters are cooked right over an open flame on the half shell, arriving at your table sizzling, drenched in a rich garlic butter sauce, and topped with a bubbly crust of melted Parmesan or Romano cheese.
Smoky Bacon & Smoked Gouda: A rich coastal favorite featuring grilled oysters topped with crispy bacon bits, green onions, and melted smoked Gouda cheese for a savory, smoky twist.
Classic Oysters Rockefeller: Plump oysters baked under a rich, fragrant topping of minced spinach, fresh herbs, breadcrumbs, and seasoned butter.
Pecan-Crusted Delights: Combining two Southern staples, oysters are coated in finely crushed pecans and fried until crispy, offering a sweet, nutty crunch served with house-made tartar sauce.
Golden Fried or Po'Boy Style: Hand-breaded in seasoned cracker meal and fried to golden perfection. Enjoy them on a seafood platter or piled high inside a crusty French roll with sweet slaw and pickles.
Raw on the Half Shell: For the adventurous purist, ice-cold raw oysters are served with lemon wedges, tangy cocktail sauce, horseradish, or a shallot mignonette, letting their natural ocean brininess shine through.

Pro-Tips for Your First Visit

Start Cooked: If you are hesitant about texture, begin with chargrilled or fried options before trying raw oysters.
Ask Your Server: Staff at local seafood spots love helping first-timers find the right dish and house specialties.
Pair It Right: Enjoy your meal with a cold local craft beer, white wine, or a signature coastal cocktail.

For lifelong shrimp lovers, making the move to Gulf oysters is the ultimate rite of passage toward becoming a true seafood connoisseur. While shrimp offer a familiar, gentle sweetness, oysters open up a complex world of "merroir"—where every shell reflects the distinct salinity, mineral depth, and currents of its specific estuary. Transitioning from familiar favorites to savory chargrilled or ice-cold raw oysters allows you to appreciate the full spectrum of Gulf Coast gastronomy. Stepping into the world of oysters not only elevates your palate, but also connects you to the rich maritime traditions and artisanal growers that define coastal cuisine.

12 Best Books for Dog Lovers with Big Hearts

A dog can turn an ordinary walk into an expedition, a quiet house into a home, and a good story into one you carry around for years. The best books for dog lovers understand that dogs are never merely pets on the page. They are confidants, comic relief, brave companions, expert judges of character, and occasionally the sharpest nose in the room.

This reading list makes room for every kind of canine reader: the person who wants a laugh after a long day, the mystery fan who appreciates a four-legged clue, the parent sharing a chapter with a child, and the reader who does not mind keeping tissues close by. Some of these books are cozy. Some are bittersweet. All of them take the bond between people and dogs seriously.

## The Best Books for Dog Lovers, Chosen by Mood

### 1. *Dog On It* by Spencer Quinn

If your ideal mystery includes a funny narrator with excellent instincts and a tendency to be distracted by bacon, start here. Chet, a retired police dog, helps private investigator Bernie Little tackle a missing-person case. His observations are earnest, loyal, and often hilarious, while the mystery itself has enough momentum to satisfy readers who like a real whodunit.

The charm is in the partnership. Chet does not think like a person, and that is precisely why he notices what others miss. This is a fine choice for cozy mystery readers who enjoy canine perspective without giving up a smart, well-paced plot.

### 2. *The Art of Racing in the Rain* by Garth Stein

Enzo is convinced that, in another life, he may return as a human. Until then, he watches his owner, Denny, pursue racing dreams and survive more than his share of hardship. Enzo’s point of view is tender, wry, and unusually observant.

This novel asks big questions about loyalty, loss, and what it means to stand beside someone when you cannot fix what hurts them. It is not a light read throughout, but it is a meaningful one. Keep tissues nearby, then make room for the hope that runs through it.

### 3. *Because of Winn-Dixie* by Kate DiCamillo

A stray dog with a big smile brings people together in a small Florida town. That simple premise becomes a gentle, funny, and deeply felt story about loneliness, friendship, and making a place for yourself.

Young readers will find an adventure that feels warm and accessible, while adults may recognize how beautifully the book captures a community of imperfect people. Winn-Dixie is a reminder that a dog can be the reason strangers start talking and old sadness begins to loosen its grip.

### 4. *Marley & Me* by John Grogan

Marley is not a polished, perfectly trained dog. He is a force of nature with a talent for chaos, damaged furniture, and wholehearted affection. John Grogan’s memoir follows Marley through the changing seasons of a family’s life, which is why it feels so familiar to many dog owners.

The humor is broad and delightful, especially for anyone who has ever apologized for a dog’s behavior while secretly admiring its enthusiasm. The ending is emotional, as life with a beloved dog often is, but the book earns every tear with honesty.

### 5. *Where the Red Fern Grows* by Wilson Rawls

Billy Colman works hard for his two hounds, Old Dan and Little Ann, and their bond becomes the center of this classic coming-of-age novel. Set in the Ozarks, the story has adventure, determination, family love, and two dogs whose courage is unforgettable.

It is often recommended for children, but it belongs on an adult reader’s shelf too. Be aware that it deals with danger and grief in a direct way. The heartbreak is real, yet so is the book’s respect for devotion, resilience, and the lasting memories dogs leave behind.

### 6. *A Dog’s Purpose* by W. Bruce Cameron

What if a dog’s life had a purpose that continued beyond one home, one family, or even one lifetime? This imaginative novel follows a dog through several lives as he learns why he is here and what humans need most from their companions.

The premise may sound sentimental, but its appeal comes from the dog’s plainspoken voice and enduring desire to belong. Readers who enjoy stories of second chances and the idea that love has a long memory will find much to savor here.

### 7. *Travels with Charley* by John Steinbeck

John Steinbeck sets out on a journey across America with Charley, his standard poodle, riding shotgun. The trip becomes a portrait of the country, but Charley is never just scenery. He is a steady companion and a practical reason for Steinbeck to meet people he might otherwise pass by.

This is a lovely choice for readers who enjoy travel writing, literary reflection, and dogs with calm, dignified presence. It moves at a thoughtful pace, so it suits an afternoon of reading more than a race to the final page.

### 8. *The Incredible Journey* by Sheila Burnford

Two dogs and a cat travel across the Canadian wilderness to find their family in this enduring animal adventure. The journey is full of danger, loyalty, and the quiet determination that animal lovers recognize at once.

Although written for younger readers, the story has a timeless pull. It is especially good for sharing across generations, perhaps with a child old enough to handle moments of tension. The animals’ perseverance makes the happy moments feel wonderfully earned.

### 9. *The Friend* by Sigrid Nunez

This thoughtful novel begins with grief. A writer inherits a large Great Dane after the death of a friend, then finds herself sharing a small apartment and a difficult season with a dog who is grieving too.

It is not a traditional dog story, and it is not a cozy one. Still, readers who have known how a dog can offer quiet company when words fail may find it deeply moving. The book is reflective and literary, best for someone in the mood for a tender, searching read.

### 10. *All Creatures Great and Small* by James Herriot

James Herriot’s veterinary stories are packed with eccentric farmers, stubborn animals, country humor, and genuine affection for every creature in his care. Dogs appear often, but the larger pleasure is seeing animal medicine practiced with patience, skill, and humility.

The episodes are easy to dip into, making this a comforting bedside book. Readers who love animal stories with historical charm will enjoy the Yorkshire setting, while anyone curious about veterinary life will appreciate the honest mix of joy, uncertainty, and muddy boots.

### 11. *Thunder Dog* by Michael Hingson with Susy Flory

Michael Hingson’s guide dog, Roselle, led him down 78 floors of the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. Their story is extraordinary, but the book is more than one dramatic day. It explores partnership, disability, trust, and the careful training behind a guide dog’s work.

This is a powerful nonfiction choice for readers who admire working dogs and want to understand the depth of communication possible between a dog and her person. The subject matter is serious, yet Roselle’s steadiness gives the story its heart.

### 12. The *Doc and Daisy Mysteries* by Stacey Bonner Gerhart

For a lighter mystery with a Florida breeze, canine wit, and a veterinarian’s eye for animal behavior, the Doc and Daisy Mysteries offer a delightful place to settle in. Daisy narrates with a warm snout and a sharp sense of what people are up to, while Doc Sue MacVety brings professional knowledge and local connections to the case.

These stories are for readers who like their puzzles smart, their communities quirky, and their dogs fully involved in the action. Canine forensics adds a modern twist without taking away the welcoming feel of a small-town mystery.

## How to Pick the Right Dog Book for Tonight

The right choice depends on what your heart can manage. If you want laughter and clues, reach for *Dog On It* or a Doc and Daisy mystery. If you want to revisit childhood or share a story with a young reader, *Because of Winn-Dixie*, *The Incredible Journey*, and *Where the Red Fern Grows* are excellent companions.

For readers who want true stories and a deeper look at the human-animal bond, *Marley & Me*, *Thunder Dog*, and *All Creatures Great and Small* offer very different but equally sincere views. And if you are in the mood for a novel that may leave you misty-eyed but grateful, Enzo, Winn-Dixie, and the dogs of Wilson Rawls’s classic are waiting patiently.

A good dog book does not have to promise that every ending will be easy. It only needs to honor the reason dogs matter so much: they meet us where we are, make us laugh when we need it, and leave paw prints on the most memorable pages of our lives.

 As Other Internet Ventures Fail,
Sex Sites Are Raking in Millions
 By THOMAS E. WEBER, Staff Reporter for THE JOURNAL

"When rapper Ice-T auditioned firms to design his new site on the World Wide Web, everyone wanted to charge $10,000 or more for the project. Everyone except Babenet Ltd.

Babenet, of Chatsworth, Calif., promised a site so compelling that Internet users would pay to see it, and it even offered to do the job free of charge if Ice-T would agree to split the earnings. The secret ingredient: X-rated pictures on-line. And so Ice-T's "Forbidden Zone" recently opened its virtual doors, zapping images of bare, undulating bodies onto the computer screen of anyone with a credit card. "This site could make $4,000 to $6,000 a day," says Ice-T's manager, Jorge Hinojosa. "The whole adult thing," he adds, "is pretty cool.""

"When Mr. Guccione's General Media Inc. established the premium "Penthouse Live" service on-line, it turned to a more seasoned Web publisher -- 23-year-old Seth Warshavsky. His company, Internet Entertainment Group, which he formed two years ago on the bankroll he earned from running a phone-sex business, is the real operator of the Penthouse "page." 📷

Mr. Warshavsky claims IEG will hit the $20 million mark in revenue this year from about 200,000 customer accounts splayed across nearly two dozen Web sites; of that amount, about 20% goes to partners like Penthouse. Short, scrubbed and apple-cheeked, Mr. Warshavsky looks hardly old enough to shave, let alone direct a sprawling adult-entertainment operation.

A Queens, N.Y., native whose family moved to the Seattle area when he was six years old, he jumped into the phone-sex business after graduating from Bellevue High School in Bellevue, Wash., Class of '91. Soon he was processing hundreds of calls each day. In 1995, he started cruising the Internet, spotted one of the early adult sites and figured he could do better.

"People on the Internet didn't have the aggressive posture you need to market," he says.

IEG employs a staff of two dozen and leases offices in a tony downtown Seattle tower. But Mr. Warshavsky's biggest single revenue generator -- an offering that has the entire adult-Web industry abuzz -- springs from an operation several minutes away. There, behind a locked door at a converted warehouse a few blocks from the Kingdome, women hired by IEG cavort nude before video cameras beaming their images out onto the Web."

""The adult firms are simply more willing to try new technologies," says Marc H. Bell of Bell Technology Group Ltd., a New York firm that provides Internet services to businesses. His mainstream clients include MSNBC, the Web site jointly run by Microsoft Corp. and General Electric Co.'s NBC network, but when he wants to recommend something new, "we go to the 'adult' people first." His latest project: a Web video site for Penthouse that will mimic cable television, piping different channels of adult and mainstream video over the Internet."

Later after Guccione sought protection in bankruptcy, a  European hedge fund called Absolute Capital Management—based in Majorca,  Spain, and London—acquired the bonds from Cerberus. Today, the  three hedge funds own a first mortgage on all of the assets of  Penthouse. Laurus has reportedly sold the mansion for $59 million in  late 2006. Galanis reportedly introduced and structured the initial Post  Advisory transaction, the Laurus/Alexandre transaction and the Molina  investment in order to restructure the company and preserve the common  stock. In May 2007, the SEC settled a suit brought against Galanis  and Samel for alleged fraud and financial misreporting. In the  settlement, no guilt was admitted, while the settlement resolves the  SEC's accusations that General Media used an unauthorized electronic  signature of Bob Guccione, the magazine's former chief executive  officer, to meet Sarbanes-Oxley-law certification requirements in its  2003 first-quarter report.[7] 
 Bankruptcy 
 
 Per SEC  filings, General Media defaulted on a $1.3 million payment on its $50  million in outstanding bonds. As a result, the bondholders had a right  to take control of the company unless General Media sought protection  under the federal bankruptcy laws.[8] 
 
 On August 12, 2003,  General Media, the parent company of the magazine, filed for Chapter 11  bankruptcy protection. Immediately upon filing, Cerberus Capital  management entered into a $5 million debtor-in-possession credit line  with General Media to provide General Media working capital.[9][10] In  October 2003, it was announced that Penthouse magazine was being put up  for sale as part of a deal with its creditors. On November 13, 2004,  Guccione resigned as Chairman and CEO of Penthouse International, the  parent of General Media. 
 
 General Media later filed a plan of  reorganization that ceded control to the bondholders, but then withdrew  this plan and filed a new plan that would have resulted in the equity  holders maintaining control of the company.[8] Also, the parties  acquired the Guccione mansion from the foreclosing lenders and reached  agreement with Guccione to lease him the home for $1 per year for the  rest of his life.[11] 
 
 Given the enormous recognition for the  Penthouse brand, financier Marc H. Bell, a high-net-worth South-Florida  real-estate developer and founder of the Globix Corporation, a  once-public Internet-hosting company, formed a partnership for the  acquisition, called it PET Capital Partners (as in, "pet of the  month")[12] then led his team in amassing 89 percent of the magazine's  $50 million in bond obligations. "We didn't buy the company, we bought  the debt," says Bell. 
 
 The bankruptcy challenges between the  bondholders and the shareholders continued through four official plans  of reorganization and substantial litigation. Ultimately, the bondholder  plan of PET Capital Partner group was confirmed by the court. However,  the plan could not close without the settlement of the outstanding  litigation between the parties. 
 
 On September 28, 2004, the  Molina parties agreed to dismiss their claims and consent to the  transaction. According to SEC filings, simultaneously Care Concepts paid  PET Capital Partners $16.45 million[13] in cash for 39.3% of Penthouse  Media Group.[14] Penthouse International paid an additional $1,000,000.  Molina released his claims in consideration for return of a $10 million  promissory note due to PET Capital Partners. 
 
 On October 4,  2004, General Media emerged from bankruptcy and was renamed the  Penthouse Media Group. It is now owned by three investors: Bell, Daniel  Staton, a South Florida investor with diverse investment properties,  ranging from Broadway shows (e.g. Jersey Boys, Hairspray, and August:  Osage County)[15] to Build-a-Bear stores, and a member of the board of  directors of Public Storage, Inc., (NYSE: PSA), and Absolute Capital  Management, run by Florian Homm, a German hedge-fund manager, who lives  on the Spanish island of Majorca. Bell was reportedly solicited for  capital by an officer of General Media but elected to buy the bonds and  attempt to foreclose.[16] Bell was quoted in South Florida CEO Magazine  in June 2004 as saying "They were in bankruptcy, their bonds were  trading for pennies and nobody wanted the company," says Bell. "It was  going to be liquidated and we figured it was a great buy." 
 
 In  August 2005, PET Capital Partners completed a financing with each of  Post Advisory, Canyon Capital, and Satellite for $40 million. According  to SEC-filed documents dated August 31, 2005, signed by Marc Bell as  President, Jefferies and Company represented Penthouse in the private  placement of new debt. According to the filing, payments were made to  directors and officers of $14,502,901 and "payments to others" were  $11,710,965.38, leaving the company with working capital of  $11,441,218.59.

On February 23, 2020 a woman in Winter Park, Florida zipped her boyfriend into a suitcase during what she later called a drunken game of hide and seek. When he started screaming that he couldn't breathe, she picked up her phone and pressed record.

Sarah Boone told police they'd been drinking all night and she thought it would be funny if Jorge Torres climbed inside. He only weighed 103 pounds, so he fit. Then she went upstairs and fell asleep, sure he could get himself out.

In the morning she remembered the suitcase, unzipped it and found him dead.

Then detectives went through her phone. In the video below, played for the jury, you hear Jorge calling her name again and again, crying and begging and telling her he can't breathe, while she laughs on the other side of the zipper and tells him "f*ck you" over and over.

"Yeah, that's what you do when you choke me."

The prosecutor said she kept him in there on purpose "to terrorize him." Sarah claimed Jorge had abused her for years and that she was the real victim. Before the trial she was offered 15 years if she pleaded guilty to manslaughter, and she turned it down.

The jury needed about 90 minutes to convict her of murder, and the judge gave her life.

At sentencing she told the court, "I forgive myself for falling in love with a monster." Jorge's sister had her own answer: "Sarah deserves to rot in jail."

She turned down 15 years and got life. Was she an abused woman who snapped for one night, or someone who enjoyed every second of that video?
