text:
Jason Calacanis told you to sell Bitcoin for AI. 

Bittensor's own cofounder just called that idea offensive.

That is the most surprising thing to come out of this week's Novelty Search, the weekly Bittensor call hosted by cofounder Const and Mark Jeffrey.

But it is not the only thing.

In under an hour, they covered Bitcoin, quantum computers, a new wallet upgrade, privacy, which subnets break through first, and why the price looks ugly while the network looks stronger than ever.

Here is all of it, step by step, in plain English.

Step 1: The tweet that started it

Earlier this week, Jason Calacanis posted that Bitcoin will never break its all time high again. He called it a dead network and told people to rotate into AI instead.

Then he followed up with something along the lines of buy $TAO.

You would expect Bittensor's leadership to celebrate that. They did the opposite.

Const said he wanted to reply, but his wife stopped him. Her words: "Don't touch that dynamite."

Mark, who is friends with Jason, joked that people came at him like his dog had peed in their yard.

His answer: "That's not my dog. It's a wild wolf."

Step 2: Why Bittensor defends Bitcoin

Const was clear. He thinks it matters more for humanity that Bitcoin survives than almost anything else in crypto.

His reasoning is simple.

Bitcoin was not built inside Silicon Valley. It was not venture funded. Nobody owns it.

That neutrality is the whole point. If Bitcoin had come out of a San Francisco startup, countries like China or Russia would never accept it as a neutral reserve asset.

Because it belongs to no one, it can still become digital gold for everyone.

And that potential is what funds the rest of the industry.

If Bitcoin loses, Const argued, everything built on top of crypto loses with it. Ethereum, Solana, and yes, Bittensor too.

Mark put it in one line: "Bitcoin is the primary asset, and everything else is secondary, including us."

Step 3: Bittensor is not trying to replace Bitcoin

People often call Bittensor "the Bitcoin of AI." Const flipped it.

He sees Bittensor as "the AI of Bitcoin."

It borrows Bitcoin's ideas, like a fixed supply and open mining, and points them at useful AI work. It is not trying to become the world's reserve currency.

He contrasted that with projects trying to out mine Bitcoin and replace it. His view: you can never recreate Bitcoin's neutral, ownerless start. Trying is pointless.

So when someone asks, "What do you need Bitcoin for when you have TAO?", his answer was blunt. He finds the question offensive.

Step 4: Scarcity and abundance, the yin and yang

This was one of the best ideas on the call.

AI and Bitcoin are opposites.

• AI makes everything abundant and changeable
• Bitcoin makes one thing perfectly scarce and unchangeable

AI is sold as an exciting future with a scary downside. Bitcoin is sold as a scary present with a hopeful future.

You need both.

Const went further. AI will create enormous wealth, but it could also widen the gap between the people who control it and everyone else.

In that world, a money with only 21 million units that nobody can print becomes more important, not less. Nobody can raise a trillion dollars and dilute your share of it.

His point: the Bitcoin thesis is quietly getting stronger every day the AI boom accelerates.

Step 5: The quantum problem, explained simply

Now to the biggest product news.

Every crypto wallet is protected by math. A powerful enough future quantum computer could, in theory, break that math and forge your signature.

Here is the part most people do not know. Bitcoin is better protected than most chains.

When you receive Bitcoin, the network only sees a scrambled version of your key, called a hash. Your real key only appears when you spend.

An attacker would have to break two things at once.

Most other chains, including Bittensor until now, show the raw key on chain at all times. If that math ever breaks, those wallets are exposed.

Step 6: What Bittensor just built

The Bittensor team built two layers of protection.

Layer one: hashed wallets.

You can swap any key on Bittensor into a hashed key. Your address stays the same. Explorers and the command line tool work the same.

The difference happens under the hood. Your real signing key stays off chain, and it gets replaced with a fresh one every time you sign a transaction.

That gives Bittensor wallets the same kind of protection Bitcoin has.

Layer two: quantum resistant signatures.

Bittensor also added two newer signature types, ML DSA and Falcon, which are designed to survive quantum attacks.

You can combine them in a multisig wallet that also sits behind a hash. To break it, an attacker would need to break several different kinds of math at the same time.

Const went out on a limb and said this could make Bittensor wallets the most secure in crypto.

But he added a big asterisk himself.

• The chain's own node keys have not been migrated yet
• Bittensor is not as decentralised as Bitcoin
• You only get the protection if you actually move to the new wallet type

Step 7: What you should actually do

For almost everyone, the answer is calm and simple.

When the upgrade is live in your wallet, consider moving your larger holdings to a hashed wallet. Small mining wallets matter much less.

As Const joked, if someone is powerful enough to break the internet, they are probably not going after your miner on a small subnet.

Nothing is forced.

Ignore anyone telling you to rush or send funds anywhere. Wait for official wallet and tool updates.

He also reminded everyone why this is not just a crypto problem. If that math breaks, email, online banking, and shopping all break with it. It would feel like 1993 overnight.

Step 8: Will Bittensor add privacy?

Mark asked if Bittensor would add Zcash style private transactions.

Const said it is technically possible. They have already looked at how to do it.

But he leans against it.

His view is that Bittensor works best as a transparent system where everyone can see who earns what. That openness makes it harder to cheat, which is the whole point of a fair AI network.

Mark agreed with him.

If you want a digital Swiss vault, use Zcash. Bittensor is doing AI.

And if someone really wants privacy, they can bridge their TAO elsewhere anyway.

Step 9: Which subnets break through first

Mark's view is that Bittensor wins the way Ethereum did. One to three standout subnets reach a billion dollars in market cap and pull the whole ecosystem forward.

And it now looks like inference will be first, meaning subnets that serve AI models to users.

Two trends are behind that.

Trend one: frontier models only stay ahead for about five weeks before an open model catches up. After that, value goes to whoever serves it cheapest without losing quality.

Trend two: big centralized compute companies like CoreWeave carry heavy debt with fixed contracts and variable financing. If rates move against them, they get squeezed.

Bittensor miners do not carry that risk. They plug in machines and supply compute on demand, the same way Bitcoin miners do.

The world, as Mark put it, reorganized itself in Bittensor's favor.

Step 10: The hard part right now

Const was honest about the pain.

Demand for top GPUs is exploding. Because Bittensor miners rent compute at today's prices, miners are paying roughly twice as much as before.

Unlike CoreWeave, the network cannot raise a big pile of capital and lock in cheap capacity ahead of time.

But he sees the other side of the cycle coming. When the buildout overshoots and there is too much compute, Bittensor's open markets get to soak up all that excess supply.

Survive the squeeze, and the network comes out stronger.

Step 11: Why research subnets look quiet

Commodity subnets like inference and compute rental were always going to earn first. The problem is obvious, and the work is about efficiency.

Research subnets are different. They look like nothing is happening until suddenly everything works.

Const gave an example.

Subnet 97, Ingot, switched to model quantisation, which shrinks AI models so they run on smaller machines. 

Within about a week, he said, its miners produced the best model you can run on a MacBook, beating a well funded team of Stanford and DeepMind alumni.

He also pointed to subnets 10 and 14, which now turn money into inference optimisation. 

Their next challenge is turning that into steady paying customers.

Step 12: The ugly price and the strong network

This was the emotional close of the call.

Const admitted the price is ugly. But he called this the most aligned and best performing moment in Bittensor's history.

His claim: almost no one in crypto produces real revenue except Bittensor and Hyperliquid.

Mark compared it to Jeff Bezos watching Amazon's stock fall 95% while every internal metric kept climbing.

Bezos knew it would come back. He just did not know when.

That is exactly how Mark says he feels watching the subnets today.

My read on all of this

The headline is not the quantum upgrade, even though it is a real and meaningful step.

The headline is the stance.

When a well known investor told the world to sell Bitcoin and buy TAO, the people building TAO refused the compliment. They chose to defend the asset their whole industry stands on.

That tells you how they see Bittensor. Not as a Bitcoin killer, but as a productive network built on Bitcoin's ideas, chasing real revenue instead of memes.

Agree or disagree with their bullishness, that is a more serious pitch than most of this market offers.

Do you see $TAO as a rival to Bitcoin, or as the AI layer built on its ideas?

Beautyon has repeatedly criticized Big Brother Watch (BBW, directed by Silkie Carlo) over several years, mainly for focusing on complaints, campaigns, and petitions without promoting practical technical solutions (VPNs, Bitcoin wallets, Signal, device region changes, etc.).

He often labels them (along with Liberty) as ineffective “Opposition Culture,” “pressure-valve” organizations, controlled opposition, or “Carlo’s Clowns,” arguing they keep people inert rather than promoting freely available and totally effective real privacy/protection tools.

Recent / Notable Posts

29 Oct 2026 (quoting a BBW post on Ofcom/social media ID plans): Calls it “drivel,” refers to them as “Carlo’s Clowns refusing once again to disseminate tools that completely render moot OfCom’s evil plans. Totally wortless.” Recommends ProtonVPN as the simple fix and criticizes the lack of actionable advice.

16 Jun 2026: In a long post on scale of UK restrictions and tech solutions, refers to “Big Brother Watch and all the other deliberately ineffective, purposely failing pressure valve organizations designed to keep INGSOCs inert, in their lanes and ineffective.”

27 May 2026: “Liberty and Big Brother Watch are two examples of the Opposition Culture that exists only to complain and point out, but never to solve.”

23 May 2026 (replying to a post about iPhone ID requirements): “Fear-mongering gibberish. Failing to provide the solution is part of the problem and the ‘Opposition Culture’ of INGSOC, as you’ve seen with the utterly worthless Big Brother Watch and Liberty. Flush them all down the loo!”

1 Aug 2025 (quoting BBW on content blocking): “BBW warned on this, but didn’t raise a finger to prepare anyone by telling them how to use a VPN. All they do is warn, while refusing to promote a single tool that will completely solve every problem they falsely claim to be concerned about. Only a fool believes they’re genuine.”

16 May 2025 (quoting BBW on encryption/Apple order): Argues BBW should publish step-by-step instructions (set iPhone region to USA, use Proton Mail/VPN, Signal, Ethical Bitcoin wallets like Proton Wallet/Wallet of Satoshi/Blockstream Green). Claims with ~123k followers they could drive mass adoption; questions why they won’t.

22 Apr 2025 (quoting BBW on government access to benefit bank accounts): Advocates mass Bitcoin adoption via wallets like Green Address; asks why BBW won’t run a viral campaign for it as a permanent solution to bank surveillance/exfiltration.

7 May 2025 (quoting BBW on Counter Disinformation Unit): “No link to [VPN/example]. No link to Proton VPN... BBW is a perpetual waterfall of FAIL.”

Earlier Examples

Feb 2024 (quoting BBW on facial recognition in dating apps): Distinguishes private-company data practices from state compulsion; calls BBW “totally worthless, confused, directionless and impotent... exist only to collect salaries.” Notes tools like WhatsApp/Signal + Bitcoin make their role obsolete, which is why they won’t promote them.

Jan 2024 (quoting BBW petition on bank spying): Contrasts petition-signing with a hypothetical viral Bitcoin (Wallet of Satoshi) campaign that could take tens of millions off traditional banking; calls them “impotent and worthless protest class... sole utility is virtue signalling.” Suggests they avoid solutions because success would put them out of a job.

Sep 2024 (various quotes of BBW posts on loyalty cards, algorithms, workplace surveillance): Accuses them of computer illiteracy, conflating private voluntary practices with state compulsion, withholding solutions, and being “dreadfully inadequate” or not genuine.

2023–2013: Similar themes, including that the Online Safety Bill won’t end end-to-end encryption (apps remain available via other means), “Fight Back” is meaningless, they don’t recommend encryption tools, and they function as controlled opposition.

Consistent critique: BBW identifies problems (surveillance, facial recognition, encryption threats, digital ID, bank access, etc.) and runs campaigns/petitions/legal actions, but does not teach or amplify free, widely available and completely effective technical workarounds that render many of those threats ineffective at the individual or mass level. He repeatedly offers examples of the concrete alternatives they omit.

text:
NQ Pre-Market Plan | Fri 10/30/2026 | ~5:45 AM CST

ICT + Japanese candlestick confirmation only.
Trade the level, not the narrative.

Charts first; news is the catalyst that resolves the range.

Macro
NQ is trading ~28,860–28,920 overnight (roughly –640 to –700 pts / –2.2 to –2.4% from yesterday’s $29,562 settlement).
Overnight range so far: low ~28,821–28,823, high ~29,180.
Yesterday’s session (10/29) delivered the post-FOMC continuation lower after the red-folder cluster; all prior bearish targets were tagged and price settled near 29,562 after probing the 29,100–29,200 area.
The past 24 hours have been volatile as the market digested the FOMC hold and Thursday’s data. 28,850 is the newfound support.

FOMC outcome (10/28): Hold at 3.75–4.00% by 10-2 vote. Dissents from Cook and Hammack preferred a 25 bp hike. Statement upgraded growth language to “strong” pace, inflation “remains elevated,” data-dependent framing. December hike remains the base case (futures pricing roughly 65–80%+ probability of a 25 bp move, depending on the source and timing).

Oil firm on Middle East supply headlines: 
WTI ~$104, Brent ~$113.

Today (CST) — Red-Folder / Data Window
Primary release is Employment Cost Index (ECI) for Q3 at 7:30 AM CST / 8:30 AM ET. Forecast ~0.8% q/q (previous ~0.9%). Chicago PMI follows at 8:45 AM CST. BOJ decision earlier in the Asian session (hold expected).

Consensus ballpark for ECI is a modest cooling from the prior print. Expect possible widened spreads around the release, though the magnitude is typically smaller than yesterday’s GDP/PCE cluster. The first move can be a knee-jerk that partly reverses once the print is absorbed relative to wages, inflation, and the still-elevated December hike pricing.

ECI matters as a labor-cost gauge that feeds into the inflation outlook the Fed is watching after Thursday’s data. An in-line or slightly cooler print keeps the current narrative intact; a hotter print would reinforce hawkish leanings.

Scenarios

In line (ECI ~0.8%):
Confirms the post-FOMC / post-PCE backdrop. Likely keeps yields relatively anchored and supports range-bound to modest bounce attempts from current levels. December hike stays the base case.

Hotter (ECI 0.9%+ or upside surprise):
Supports the hawks who dissented. Expect higher yields, firmer dollar, and renewed pressure on growth/tech. Bounce attempts from 28,850 become more fragile; risk of extension lower increases.

Cooler (ECI ≤0.7%):
Modest relief. Yields and dollar can ease slightly; supports a bounce toward 29,000. Unlikely to fully remove December hike odds but softens the near-term pressure.

How it interacts with yesterday’s prints:
Hot ECI after strong GDP/hotter-leaning PCE reinforces the hawkish combination. Cooler ECI after mixed growth/inflation data offers a “soft landing” relief bounce window.

This is the digestion window after yesterday’s FOMC aftermath and red-folder cluster. Expect potential expansion once the ECI print and tone are clear. Pre-data chop inside the overnight range is the base case until displacement appears.
Holding or managing prior short exposure that delivered the bearish targets. No new aggressive entries until after the 7:30 AM data and clear post-news structure. Sitting on hands is the active plan until then.

ICT Framework
HTF remains bearish-to-neutral with lower highs intact off the early-October ATH area near 31,600. 29,000 zone continues as a major multi-session reference / prior liquidity draw. Price is currently trading at the 28,850 newfound support after yesterday’s expansion lower. Dealing range reference: recent swing highs near 29,500–29,800 vs overnight/session lows around 28,820–28,850. Price is now in the lower portion of the recent multi-session range.

Structure notes: Post-FOMC + Thursday data produced the downside displacement. Overnight action is probing the 28,850 zone. 15m/5m SMTs and IFVG/FVG development are confluence only once post-data displacement appears.
Liquidity
• SSL: 28,850 zone (newfound support) · 28,820 overnight low · 28,500–28,600 extension
• BSL: 29,000 (major retest / bounce target) · 29,100–29,200 · 29,300 · 29,500–29,562 prior settlement area · higher toward 29,775–29,900

Time windows: NY AM Killzone 6:00–9:00 AM CT · Cash open 8:30 · Silver Bullet 9:00–10:00. Priority is post-7:30 AM ECI for clean displacement. Model: Power of Three / Judas possible around the data release or cash open. Watching for sweep of either side of the overnight range before directional intent.
Levels of the Day
28,850 (newfound support) · 28,820 (overnight low) · 29,000 (bounce target) · 29,100–29,200 · 29,300 · 29,500–29,562 · 29,775–29,900 (higher retest)

Bullish Setups

A. Post-data MSS + FVG / IFVG acceptance above 28,900–29,000
ECI comes in constructive (in-line or cooler). Price shows bullish market structure shift + displacement that leaves a bullish FVG. 5-min close and acceptance higher with clear displacement, including candle closure back over 28,900–29,000.

Entry: Pullback into the FVG/IFVG in the OTE (62–79%).
Candle confirm: hammer / pin bar, bullish engulfing, or morning star.

Targets: TP1 29,100 → TP2 29,200 → TP3 29,300–29,500.

Invalidation: 5-min close back below the structure-shift low or failure to hold 28,850.

B. Aggressive push through 29,000 with FVG entry
After the data, price expands hard and fast through 29,000, leaving a clean bullish FVG before continuation.

Entry: Pullback into that FVG in the OTE with candle confirmation.

Targets: same as above.

Invalidation: failure to hold the FVG or close back under the displacement low.

Bearish Setups

A. Failure to reclaim 29,000 + post-data expansion lower
Price remains under 29,000. ECI (especially hotter) produces displacement down. 5-min close and acceptance lower with clear displacement.

Entry: Retest into a bearish FVG/IFVG in the OTE or right below 28,850–28,900 on the retest if it holds as resistance.

Candle confirm: shooting star, bearish engulfing, or evening star.

Targets: TP1 28,700 → TP2 28,600 → TP3 28,500.

Invalidation: 5-min close back above 28,900 or the structure-shift high.

B. Overnight low sweep + continued lower displacement
Price sweeps the overnight lows (~28,821–28,823) then shows continued bearish structure and displacement.

Entry: Retest of the sweep high or into the bearish FVG in the OTE.

Targets: same as above.

Invalidation: reclaim and close above the sweep high or 28,900.

No Trade If
Pre-data chop or doji stacking inside the overnight range. Price chopping between key levels (especially 28,820–28,900 or 28,900–29,100) with no displacement. No clean setup after the 7:30 AM data and initial reaction (knee-jerk that fails to sustain). Sitting out is a position.

PUNCHLINE: A hundred biomarkers and no doctor is a very expensive way to worry.

text:
81% of S&P 500 Stocks Rose. So Why Did the Nasdaq Fall 1.38%?

U.S. Market Recap | October 29, 2026

$GOOGL plunged 12.6%. The Nasdaq fell 1.38%, and the S&P 500 declined 0.30%. After the closing bell, disappointing reactions to $AMZN and $INTC earnings added further pressure to technology stocks.

Yet 406 of the S&P 500’s 503 constituents finished higher. The Russell 2000 gained 1.01%, and nine of the S&P 500’s eleven sectors advanced.

This wasn’t a market where investors were selling everything. It was a market where a relatively small group of heavily weighted companies overwhelmed much broader gains.

I believe that distinction matters. The AI investment cycle remains strong, but investors are becoming more selective about which companies can turn growth into sustainable earnings and cash flow.

The bigger question is whether this represents the beginning of healthier market leadership—or merely a temporary rotation away from expensive technology stocks.

1. THE MARKET WAS STRONGER THAN THE INDEX SUGGESTED

Thursday’s closing figures:

S&P 500: 7,720.39 (-0.30%)
Nasdaq Composite: 26,184.72 (-1.38%)
Dow Jones: 52,342.56 (-0.25%)
Russell 2000: 2,859.22 (+1.01%)

The explanation lies in market-capitalization weighting.

Companies such as Alphabet represent a substantial portion of the major indexes. When a few mega-cap stocks experience sharp declines, their losses can offset gains across hundreds of smaller companies.

On October 29, healthcare, financials, consumer-related businesses, and several traditional industries showed relative strength. Meanwhile, large internet companies, software stocks, and parts of the semiconductor sector faced intense selling pressure.

This is why market breadth matters.

An index measures the performance of its constituents according to its weighting methodology. Market breadth helps reveal how widely gains or losses are distributed.

When 81% of S&P 500 constituents rise but the index falls, the average stock is telling a different story from the headline index.

I’m encouraged by that divergence. A bull market supported by a broader range of profitable businesses would be healthier than one dependent on a handful of technology giants.

However, one session isn’t enough to confirm a sustained rotation. We still need evidence that improving breadth persists alongside stable earnings expectations and reasonable valuations.

2. STRONG GDP, STICKY INFLATION: A COMPLICATED MACRO BACKDROP

The U.S. economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in Q3, accelerating from 2.2% in Q2. Consumer spending, business investment, and government expenditures contributed to that expansion.

Those figures don’t suggest an economy entering an immediate broad-based contraction.

Inflation tells a less comfortable story.

September headline PCE inflation reached 3.6% year over year, while core PCE remained at 3.1%, above the Federal Reserve’s 2% objective.

An especially interesting detail was consumer spending. Nominal personal consumption expenditures increased 0.5% month over month, but inflation-adjusted spending was essentially flat.

Americans spent more dollars without purchasing meaningfully more goods and services.

That’s an important distinction for future corporate earnings. Nominal revenue can rise because of higher prices even when real demand is stagnating.

The Fed maintained its policy rate at 3.75%–4.00% on October 28. Strong economic growth gives policymakers room to remain restrictive, while persistent inflation makes rapid monetary easing harder to justify.

For equities, this creates competing forces. Economic resilience can support earnings, but elevated discount rates place pressure on expensive valuations and long-duration growth investments.

I’m not bearish simply because interest rates remain elevated. But I expect companies with strong balance sheets, pricing power, and reliable cash generation to command an increasing premium over businesses whose investment cases depend heavily on future financing.

3. AMAZON: RECORD OPERATING MARGINS, NEGATIVE FREE CASH FLOW

Amazon’s earnings illustrated the central tension facing the AI economy.

$AMZN reported Q3 revenue of $201.9B, up 12% year over year. Operating income increased to $28.1B, producing a record 13.9% operating margin.

AWS delivered particularly impressive results. Revenue climbed 39.3% to $46B, its fastest growth in nearly five years, while operating profit reached $17.8B, up approximately 56%.

These numbers demonstrate that AI and cloud infrastructure demand is translating into actual operating earnings.

CEO Andy Jassy also projected AWS revenue growth above 40% in both 2027 and 2028. That’s a remarkable ambition for a business already operating at a $184B annualized revenue run rate, but it remains a management forecast rather than a guaranteed outcome.

The problem is cash conversion.

Over the trailing twelve months, Amazon generated $168.3B in operating cash flow, up 29%. Yet free cash flow fell to approximately -$42.4B as infrastructure investment accelerated.

Management continues to expect around $220B in cash capital expenditures for 2026.

Amazon isn’t losing money because AWS is unprofitable. AWS is highly profitable. The issue is that the company is committing enormous amounts of capital today to support expected demand over the coming years.

At the same time, Q3 EPS of $1.89 came in below the approximately $1.96 consensus, while the $240B–$247B Q4 revenue guidance was slightly below market expectations at its midpoint.

Year-over-year EPS comparisons also require care because last year’s results benefited from substantial investment gains related to Anthropic.

My view on Amazon remains positive over the long term. AWS has scale, customer relationships, technological capabilities, and substantial earnings power.

But the investment case increasingly depends on the timing of returns. If AWS sustains growth near management’s forecasts, today’s investment cycle could support significantly higher future earnings. If capital requirements keep rising faster than cash generation, shareholders may face a longer payback period than current valuations imply.

I would focus less on whether Amazon beats quarterly revenue estimates by a fraction of a percent and more on whether incremental AWS profits can eventually outgrow the capital required to produce them.

4. INTEL: A REAL SERVER RECOVERY, BUT AN UNFINISHED TURNAROUND

Intel’s earnings presented a different contradiction.

$INTC reported Q3 revenue of $16.51B, up 21%, with adjusted EPS of $0.52. Its Data Center & AI division generated $7.32B in revenue, an increase of 78% year over year.

DCAI operating profit reached $3.04B, representing a 41.5% operating margin.

That is meaningful operating progress. AI infrastructure requires general-purpose CPUs alongside accelerators, and Intel is benefiting from the expansion of server computing demand.

But the market wasn’t primarily concerned about the quarter that just ended.

Intel projected Q4 revenue of $15B–$16B, compared with Wall Street expectations around $17.07B. Adjusted gross margin is expected to decline from 44.1% to 38%.

An accident at Intel’s Israeli manufacturing facility is expected to reduce Q4 revenue by approximately $300M and gross margin by about two percentage points.

That disruption is significant, but it cannot explain the entire guidance shortfall. Even after adding back the estimated lost revenue, the Q4 midpoint remains materially below consensus.

PC demand remains weak, elevated memory prices are creating additional pressure, and manufacturing capacity constraints continue to affect production economics.

Meanwhile, Intel Foundry’s quarterly operating loss narrowed to approximately $1.85B. That’s an improvement, but the business remains far from sustained profitability.

I remain constructive on Intel’s server CPU recovery. However, I see the foundry turnaround as a separate, higher-risk investment proposition that still requires evidence of external customer demand, successful advanced-node production, and acceptable returns on capital.

A 20% after-hours selloff doesn’t erase the progress in DCAI. Equally, strong DCAI results don’t eliminate the financial risks associated with manufacturing expansion.

The long-term opportunity is real, but the next few quarters must show that improving product demand can translate into stronger consolidated margins and ultimately sustainable free cash flow.

5. AI’S NEW DILEMMA: SPENDING MORE OR EARNING MORE?

The most important development across recent technology earnings is a change in what investors are willing to reward.

For much of the AI investment cycle, rising capital expenditures were interpreted as evidence of strong future demand.

That logic hasn’t disappeared, but the market is starting to examine the other side of the transaction.

Alphabet’s latest results offer a clear example.

$GOOGL increased Google Cloud revenue 103% to $30.7B. Yet the company generated approximately $42.3B in operating cash flow against $51.4B in cash capital expenditures, resulting in quarterly free cash flow of roughly -$9.1B.

Search revenue growth also moderated to 12%, raising questions about whether AI-related engagement will translate into equally strong advertising economics.

Microsoft presents a different financial profile.

$MSFT reported Azure growth of 48% and generated $58B in operating cash flow. After approximately $39.4B in cash spending on property and equipment, simple quarterly free cash flow remained positive at roughly $18.6B.

Microsoft also announced a $25B senior unsecured debt offering on October 29. Borrowing despite positive free cash flow isn’t necessarily evidence of financial distress; financing decisions can reflect capital allocation, liquidity management, and the relative cost of debt.

The comparison doesn’t prove that Microsoft’s AI investments are more profitable than Google’s. The companies have different business models, investment schedules, and cash-flow dynamics.

It does show that the financial burden of AI expansion is distributed unevenly.

There’s also a broader industry dilemma.

If hyperscalers continue raising capital expenditures, semiconductor, memory, optical networking, power equipment, and data-center suppliers may enjoy sustained demand.

But excessive spending can pressure the customers’ free cash flow and future returns.

If hyperscalers eventually slow infrastructure investment to improve cash generation, their suppliers could face weaker orders and lower growth expectations.

The solution isn’t simply to stop investing. It’s to improve the productivity and profitability of each incremental dollar deployed.

Three metrics will become increasingly important: revenue growth, free cash flow, and return on invested capital.

The strongest businesses will ultimately need to demonstrate all three—not just exceptional demand.

6. GROWTH ISN’T LIMITED TO BIG TECH

Thursday’s market action also demonstrated that strong business performance exists outside the largest AI platforms.

Eli Lilly ($LLY) reported Q3 revenue of $24.4B, up 39%, supported by demand for Mounjaro and Zepbound. The company raised its full-year revenue outlook to $91B–$92B.

The underlying demand picture is encouraging: volume increased 53%, more than offsetting a 15% decline in realized prices.

However, Q3 results also included approximately $900M of favorable milestone and rebate-related items. Those benefits shouldn’t automatically be treated as recurring earnings.

The investment opportunity lies in sustained prescription growth, manufacturing scale, and the company’s ability to manage pricing pressure—not simply the headline revenue beat.

Storage is another area displaying exceptional demand.

Sandisk ($SNDK) reported fiscal Q1 2027 revenue of $11.03B, up 23% sequentially. Data-center revenue increased 61% quarter over quarter to $4.80B, highlighting strong demand across AI infrastructure.

The company also repurchased approximately $5B of stock and announced an 8-for-1 share split.

I view the underlying storage demand as more important than the split itself. A stock split changes the number of shares and the price per share, not the company’s total economic value.

Samsung reported record memory business revenue and operating profit, reinforcing the strength of the current memory cycle. At the same time, weaker economics in other divisions showed how differently business segments can perform within a single company.

These results support an important conclusion: AI demand is creating genuine earnings opportunities across hardware and infrastructure, even while investors reassess the valuations of major AI spenders.

But memory remains cyclical. Exceptional margins and pricing power should not be assumed permanent.

7. THE LONG-TERM BULL CASE: WEAKER TECH DOESN’T MEAN WEAKER AMERICA

Despite the recent technology selloff, I remain bullish on the longer-term outlook for U.S. equities.

The evidence is broader than AI enthusiasm.

First, economic growth remains resilient. A 3.4% annualized GDP expansion provides a stronger earnings backdrop than investors would expect in a contracting economy.

Second, corporate profits continue to hold up. According to LSEG data cited by Reuters on October 29, approximately 81% of the 253 S&P 500 companies that had reported earnings exceeded analyst expectations. Aggregate Q3 earnings growth was expected to reach approximately 31%.

That doesn’t guarantee higher share prices. Markets react to expectations, guidance, and valuations, not simply whether earnings exceed a published estimate.

Still, widespread earnings resilience is difficult to reconcile with a thesis of imminent, economy-wide corporate deterioration.

Third, major institutions continue to project long-term earnings and productivity growth.

Goldman Sachs Research forecasts S&P 500 EPS of approximately $415 in 2027 and $460 in 2028. Its outlook suggests that future index gains may depend more on earnings expansion than further valuation multiple increases.

J.P. Morgan Asset Management recently raised its projected annual return for U.S. large-cap equities to 7.5% over the next 10–15 years, citing technology adoption, productivity improvements, and resilient corporate profitability.

These are forecasts, not guarantees. Their significance is that the structural growth case remains credible even when near-term earnings disappointments cause volatility.

What about the November 3 midterm elections?

Historically, post-midterm periods have often been favorable for U.S. equities. Fidelity’s analysis indicates that the S&P 500 delivered positive price returns in roughly 95% of the twelve-month periods following midterm elections since 1938, averaging around 14%.

That’s an interesting historical pattern, but not a trading signal. The sample is limited, and economic conditions differ across cycles.

There is no financial rule requiring the market to wait until after Election Day to recover. Equities can rebound before the election, continue falling afterward, or move independently of the political calendar.

I believe earnings revisions, inflation, interest rates, and capital returns will matter considerably more to the sustainability of the next rally.

FINAL OUTLOOK

October 29 wasn’t evidence that the AI boom has ended. It was evidence that investors are becoming less willing to reward growth without examining its cost.

Alphabet’s selloff reflects concerns about AI capital intensity and Search monetization. Amazon’s results show exceptional AWS demand alongside increasingly negative free cash flow. Intel demonstrates that a strong server recovery can coexist with serious manufacturing and execution challenges.

Meanwhile, healthcare, consumer businesses, and parts of the storage industry are showing that earnings growth extends beyond a handful of mega-cap technology companies.

I remain bullish on the long-term U.S. equity market, but I expect the next phase to be more selective.

Companies with strong competitive advantages, sustainable earnings growth, and improving returns on capital should be better positioned than those relying primarily on ambitious revenue projections.

The risks are real: persistent inflation, expensive valuations, earnings downgrades, and the possibility that AI infrastructure spending fails to generate expected returns.

But a market in which most stocks rise while a few giants fall doesn’t look like a universal rejection of risk. It looks like investors are beginning to distinguish between different sources of growth.

For long-term investors, that distinction may create opportunities well before the headlines turn optimistic again.

The next stage of this bull market may be driven less by how much companies spend on AI—and more by how much value they ultimately create from it.

Stay curious. Stay bullish.

Chinese Stock Market Hits Record-Long Weekly Losing Streak: CSI 300 Declines for 12 Consecutive Weeks Amid AI Sell-off and Weak Domestic Demand

The Record: A 12-Week Losing Streak—The Longest Since 2005

For the week ending October 30, 2026, the CSI 300 Index closed lower for the twelfth consecutive week, marking its longest weekly losing streak since the index’s inception in 2005. The previous record of eleven weeks was surpassed during the week ending October 23. The cumulative decline over these twelve weeks stands at approximately 14%, with a 7.6% drop in October alone—the largest monthly decline since July. The index has fallen more than 20% from its June high, entering technical bear market territory. In terms of market capitalization, the Chinese stock market has shed roughly $3.5 trillion since its peak in May.

The Immediate Catalyst: A Global AI Sell-off Spills Over into the A-share Market

The most severe declines have been concentrated in the technology and AI-related sectors. The CSI Artificial Intelligence Index, which tracks major Chinese AI companies, has fallen 19% over the past month. On the same trading day, the STAR 50 Index dropped 1.8%, while the optical communications sector plunged as much as 6% during morning trading. Shares of optical module manufacturer Eoptolink have fallen 46% this month, a direct reflection of the impact from a correction in the global investment cycle for AI infrastructure.

The trigger for this sell-off originated in the U.S. market, where shares of Alphabet, Amazon, and Intel fell amid concerns over AI-related spending; meanwhile, South Korea’s SK Hynix saw a decline of over 7%, with the negative sentiment rippling through to Asian tech stocks. Kenneth Fong, Head of China Internet Research at UBS, noted that the valuation models for some internet stocks now assume that heavy AI investment will become a permanent drag on profitability, with the market assigning negligible value to the potential for these AI investments to eventually generate returns.

Deeper Structural Issues: Weak Domestic Demand and a Gap in Policy Credibility

The pullback in AI stocks is merely a symptom; the underlying issue is the persistent weakness of the domestic economy. Wage growth has slowed, companies are struggling to raise prices, and household wealth has shrunk due to declining property values. Government spending actually declined during the first three quarters—a significant departure from the fiscal policy trajectory the market had anticipated at the start of the year. Investors are now left wondering: with domestic demand remaining weak, where is the room for growth in corporate sales and profits?

Intervention by the "national team"—state-backed funds—has failed to reverse the trend. Last Thursday, these funds injected $6.8 billion into the stock market, offering a brief respite from a persistent slide; however, by Tuesday, the market had fallen another 1.3%. Financial commentator Shi Shusi, as quoted by *The New York Times*, remarked: "Such interventions might help prop up the market, but they cannot shore up investor confidence." Gary Ng, a senior economist at Natixis, offered a more blunt assessment: "If the government continues to inject capital, we might see a short-term rally, but it won't be sustainable."

A Notable Historical Parallel

In December 2023, the CSI 300 Index experienced a six-week losing streak—a development then considered historic. Yet, that decline did not mark the market bottom; the index fell nearly 14% over the course of 2023, and that six-week slide proved to be a prelude to further pain rather than the end of it. The current twelve-week losing streak has already far surpassed that duration, yet there is no verifiable evidence to suggest that the market is nearing a bottom. As Christopher Beddor, deputy director of China research at Gavekal Dragonomics, told *The New York Times*: "We are reaching the pain threshold where officials feel they must intervene." A pain threshold may trigger intervention, but it is no guarantee of a market turnaround.

Elon Musk offered $97.4 billion for OpenAI. Sam Altman answered in one line:

"no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want"

Exactly one tenth of the offer. Musk replied with one word. "Swindler."

The two started OpenAI together in 2015 as a nonprofit. Musk left the board in 2018 and has been fighting Altman ever since, including in court.

The bid landed in February 2025, right when OpenAI was trying to turn itself into a for-profit company. A few days later OpenAI's board rejected it unanimously. Altman's own guess was that Musk was "probably just trying to slow us down."

I don't think either of them expected a sale. Musk's offer made OpenAI's restructuring harder and more expensive. Altman's reply turned a serious legal move into a meme the whole internet shared.

Still, it's wild to watch two of the richest men in tech fight like this over a company they started together.

Who won this round, Musk or Altman?

text:
RECRUITING TALK: STARS, NO STARS & NIL 🏈

As a high school coach, I want players and parents to understand this: recruiting stars can help open doors, but they don’t determine how far you can go.

Respect the players who earned those ratings. Many are outstanding athletes who put in serious work. But understand what a star rating represents: a recruiting service’s evaluation and projection at a particular point in a player’s development.

It is not a scholarship, a starting position, a degree or a guaranteed NFL career.

And being unrated does NOT mean a college coaching staff cannot evaluate you, recruit you or offer you a scholarship.

Some players develop later. Some receive less exposure. Some haven’t been evaluated extensively. Others need to improve before they’re ready for the next level. Our job as coaches is to give an honest assessment and help each player build a realistic path.

College coaches recruit for THEIR roster. Your film, verified measurables, academics, position fit, development and character all matter. A recruiting website doesn’t make their final decision.

Want proof that an unrated player can build a professional career? Josh Allen left high school without stars, went through junior college and earned his opportunity at Wyoming. His path proves it is possible—not that it is easy or guaranteed.

Now let’s address NIL.

There is no recruiting-star requirement for a legitimate NIL opportunity.

NIL means a business compensates you for using your name, image or likeness through activities such as endorsements, promotional content or appearances. Stars may increase visibility, but businesses can also value your audience, community connections, credibility and ability to represent their brand.

An unrated player with an engaged local following and professional habits can offer value to a business. That does not guarantee a deal, and every athlete should have realistic expectations about the money involved.

Start building those habits now:

• Put quality football on film.
• Protect your grades and eligibility.
• Make your recruiting information easy to find.
• Communicate professionally.
• Build authentic community relationships.
• Create useful, consistent content.
• Follow through when you make a commitment.

Understand this distinction, too: a scholarship, third-party NIL deal and direct payment from a college are different things. An offer does not automatically include all three.

Before accepting NIL compensation, verify the rules that apply to your school, athletic association and future college. Have agreements reviewed and meet applicable reporting requirements.

My advice: choose a college where you can develop, afford your education and prepare for life. Evaluate the coaching, academics, roster and total financial package.

Football can lead to college, professional opportunities, coaching, business and relationships that last well beyond your playing days. The NFL is one possible outcome—not the only meaningful career.

text:
The flower beds were full. Phoenix, her silver bike, leaned against the wall, less used now that she had a driver’s license, but still kept polished.

My parents were not invited.

Sarah was not invited.

No one from my family came except Rebecca, who brought a lemon cake and cried when Emma opened her Penn State hoodie.

During the party, Emma stood near the place where she had fallen years before and laughed with her friends about dorm room decorations.

That was when the last piece of anger inside me finally loosened.

Not disappeared. I do not believe anger like that disappears. It becomes part of the structure, like scar tissue. But it stopped driving.

That night, after everyone left, Emma and I sat under the lanterns.

“I’m glad we stayed,” she said.

“Me too.”

“I used to think this yard belonged to what happened.”

“And now?”

She looked at the lights, the flowers, the bike, the empty plates stacked near the door.

“Now it belongs to us again.”

People sometimes ask if I regret what I did.

They do not always ask directly. They dress it up.

Do you ever think it went too far?

Do you think prison was necessary?

Was it worth losing your family?

The answer depends on what they mean by family.

If they mean the people who share my blood but defended Vanessa before Emma was even out of surgery, then yes, losing them was worth it.

If they mean the mother who called my daughter “difficult” while her ribs were broken, then yes.

If they mean the father who told me children are resilient as if resilience is a reason to tolerate violence, then yes.

If they mean relatives who had more compassion for Vanessa’s reputation than Emma’s recovery, then yes.

I do not regret losing people who required my daughter’s silence as the price of belonging.

That is not family.

That is a hostage arrangement with holiday meals.

Vanessa served longer than five years before parole became realistic again. By then, Brooklyn was nearly an adult. I heard fragments through people who did not understand that silence was a boundary, not an invitation to update me. Brooklyn struggled, then stabilized. My parents raised her with the same blind loyalty that had damaged Vanessa in the first place. Whether Brooklyn outgrew it, I do not know.

I hope she does.

That is the most generosity I can offer from a distance.

Vanessa wrote once.

The letter came through the prison system, forwarded to our attorney because the no-contact order still stood. The envelope was not opened by us. Our attorney read enough to say it contained “language of apology mixed with blame.”

That sounded exactly like Vanessa.

I told him to destroy it.

I did not need her apology. More importantly, Emma did not need it. We had spent years learning that healing did not require participation from the person who caused the wound.

Emma left for college on a hot August morning.

Her room was half-empty, her car packed with laundry baskets and plastic bins. Phoenix stayed in the garage because campus was too big and bikes got stolen. Before leaving, Emma stood beside it and ran one hand over the handlebar.

“You sure you don’t want to bring it?” I asked.

She smiled. “No. It belongs here.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means I survived here. I don’t need to carry the proof everywhere.”

I had to turn away for a second.

Derek pretended to adjust a bungee cord on the car roof, but his shoulders were shaking.

At Penn State, we helped her unpack in a dorm room that smelled like fresh paint, dust, and nervous teenagers. Her roommate had already hung fairy lights. Emma placed the framed certificate from the prosecutor’s office on her desk, not on the wall. Beside it, she placed a photo of the three of us at the beach.

No family portrait from the old days.

No Vanessa. No grandparents.

When it was time to leave, she hugged me carefully at first, out of habit, then tighter.

“My ribs are fine, Mom,” she whispered.

I laughed and cried at the same time.

“I know.”

Tehran’s Calculus: The Next War Cannot Be "Limited"—It Must Be So Costly That No Future U.S. President Would Dare Attempt It

Core Assessment: A Shift in Deterrence Logic—From "Defense" to "Punishment"

The Iranian leadership’s planning for the next round of conflict has moved beyond traditional objectives like "preventing U.S. forces from entering" or "offering a symbolic response to a limited strike." A Reuters report from October 1, 2026—citing three senior Iranian officials and one well-placed source—indicates that Tehran is preparing a "broader and more forceful" response. The scope of potential targets has expanded from U.S.-linked assets to include "nations that support U.S. military operations," and potentially even locations "outside the Middle East." Iranian commanders are now focused on target selection, geographic reach, and the tempo of operations, rather than on how to contain the scale of the conflict.

The theoretical basis for this shift, as outlined in an analysis by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, suggests that Iran’s strategy is not built around a single pressure point. Instead, it integrates several elements—selective disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, sustained missile and drone strikes, attacks on U.S. regional infrastructure, and the activation of multiple potential fronts (including a second maritime front in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait)—into a "mutually reinforcing toolkit." Closing the Strait of Hormuz in isolation would be viewed as a discrete act, likely inviting a concentrated, multinational military response; however, when integrated into a broader framework of escalation, such a move becomes both "credible and difficult to contain."

Why a "Limited War" Works in Tehran’s Favor

In an analysis from July 2026, the BBC offered a counterintuitive assessment: for Iran, a limited, ongoing conflict might actually be more advantageous than peace. The logic is as follows: under a long-term ceasefire, the U.S.-led maritime blockade would persist, sanctions would remain in place, and Iran would continue to be excluded from international energy markets. Meanwhile, regional exporters—such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar—would be able to gradually restore their normal export operations. In this scenario, Iran remains isolated while its neighbors profit.

A limited conflict alters this dynamic. Even if Iran incurs heavy military and economic costs, its interference in the Strait of Hormuz—along with the pressure exerted via the Houthis in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait—would still impact global shipping, insurance costs, and energy markets. Even a state of "limited uncertainty" compels governments, shipowners, and importers to pay heed to Iran’s demands. Tehran’s calculation is that keeping a crisis just below the threshold of all-out war is more advantageous than accepting a ceasefire that leaves existing sanctions and blockades in place.

"Zero Red Lines" and an "Asymmetric, Intense, and Decisive War"

In late October 2026, as the U.S. midterm elections approached and the Trump administration signaled the possibility of a "short and sharp" strike, the rhetoric from Iran’s senior leadership escalated further. According to an October 29 briefing by The Soufan Center, high-ranking Iranian officials described their anticipated retaliation as adhering to "zero red lines"—implying a "protracted, all-out war" with no constraints regarding timing or the selection of targets. Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior advisor to Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, wrote on social media: "We are currently in the surprise phase of a war; we will not be fighting a conventional war... This will be an asymmetric, intense, and decisive war, targeting both the strengths and weaknesses of the enemy."

This framing aligns with remarks made in September by IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi: "Should a new attack occur, our defensive and offensive operations will undergo a significant shift. We will alter the weaponry used and the geographical scope of the conflict... Our targets will no longer be the same as before. We have identified new targets that have not yet been struck."

Actual Capabilities: Strikes Already Demonstrated

These are not empty threats. Citing a Reuters report, *Pars* noted today that since the conflict began on February 28, 2026, Iran and its allies have launched at least 135 missile and drone attacks against 84 critical U.S. infrastructure targets across Persian Gulf nations. These targets include oil and gas facilities, airports, pipelines, and strategic assets linked to the U.S. military in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, and Bahrain. According to Reuters’ assessment, the precision of these strikes and the damage inflicted on key infrastructure have "disrupted Washington’s war planning and increased the economic and strategic costs for both the United States and Israel."

Through diplomatic channels, Iran has also issued a direct warning to Gulf states: should the United States launch further attacks on Iranian territory, Iran will strike vital energy infrastructure throughout the Persian Gulf region. In calls with his counterparts from Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Qatar, as well as the Chief of Army Staff of Pakistan, Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi conveyed a consistent message: "We are prepared to retaliate, but a diplomatic solution remains the best path to prevent further regional escalation and destruction." The timing of this warning—following Donald Trump’s July 28 threat to target Iran’s energy network—suggests that Tehran is seeking to raise the costs of military action by threatening Washington’s closest regional allies.

The Logic of a War of Attrition—and Its Limits

Analysis from the Carnegie Endowment points out that the logic behind Iran’s strategy of attrition is not based on a fixed timeline, but rather on "relative endurance." Tehran’s calculation is that the United States—and, to an extent, Israel—faces political, economic, and logistical constraints that make the costs of a protracted conflict increasingly prohibitive. This explains why Iran has consistently rejected the notion of a ceasefire; the objective is not to pause the conflict, but to extend it long enough to alter the adversaries' own cost-benefit calculations.

However, attrition is a two-way street. Iranian planners are well aware of this: sustained strikes can degrade infrastructure, strain command-and-control systems, and heighten the risk of internal instability. The political dimension is equally critical: the longer a war persists, the greater the need to demonstrate that the costs imposed on the adversary are translating into tangible strategic gains. Otherwise, the logic of endurance begins to falter. Carnegie’s conclusion is that the critical question is not how long Iran can sustain a war of attrition, but whether it can do so “credibly”—for if the conflict persists without any visible shift in the strategic equation, attrition risks transforming from a tool into a liability.

U.S. Options and Iranian Countermeasures

Washington’s stated posture points toward a “short, sharp” campaign—targeting Iranian infrastructure and nuclear facilities—envisioned for the period following the November 3 midterm elections. Iran’s counter-logic is clear: if the U.S. seeks a limited, controllable conflict from which it can declare victory and withdraw, Iran will ensure that outcome remains out of reach. The cost must be high enough to give any future U.S. president pause before considering another strike—not out of concern for military feasibility, but out of fear of the political price.

This strategy carries real risks: “controllable” conflicts have a habit of spiraling out of control. Yet, Tehran appears to have calculated that, given the current reality of sanctions, blockades, and economic isolation, an imperfect peace works against its interests. A controlled crisis—however painful—at least preserves a degree of leverage. Ultimately, whether this assessment holds true depends not on Tehran’s intentions, but on whether Washington and regional states are prepared to accept the costs that Iran is prepared to impose.

One thing I know about Med Twitter is that people are often attacked for saying uncomfortable truths. Many here are biased and cowardly, preferring to attack an opinion rather than admit what is obvious.

Not all medical schools are the same. A private medical school differs from a state medical school, which differs from a federal medical school. Even among federal universities, there are differences.

At UI, you need 80+ in anatomy, biochemistry and physiology to earn distinctions. 

In my school, the threshold is 70.

Someone in my senior set earned three distinctions with scores in the 70s. Had he attended UI, he would have graduated without a single distinction in those courses.

Some schools have higher academic standards, stricter assessments, bigger teaching hospitals that see more cases, higher fees and more competitive admissions. 

Others are easier to enter. A state medical school is generally easier to gain admission into than a federal one, while private medical schools can offer another route for those who can afford them.

Consider two friends who finish secondary school at 16 and both score 270 in JAMB. 

One has parents who can afford ABUAD, so he begins medical school at 16. The other cannot afford it and spends five to seven years writing JAMB to get into OAU, where his family can afford the fees.

By the time the second friend reaches his second year, the first may already have graduated and started housemanship.

And you want to tell me their struggles, opportunities and stakes are equal?

There is nothing equal about that situation. MBBS is not MBBS in every practical sense. The experiences, standards, resources and circumstances differ.

I have made this argument before, but people keep trying to blur the lines. The more we stop deceiving ourselves about these differences, the better. 

But I know some of you would rather keep deceiving yourselves. Carry on.

On October 30th we celebrate the feast of St. Marcellus the Centurion, Martyr

Marcellus was a Christian centurion in the Roman army. In the year of Our Lord 298, he and his legion were serving in what is now Tangier, Morocco. The birthday of the Emperor Maximian was being celebrated throughout the empire, with many solemn sacrifices offered to the pagan gods. Marcellus, who would normally lead his men in these sacrifices, instead cast down his equipment and symbols of rank and publicly proclaimed himself a Christian. He was imprisoned until the festivities ended, and then taken before the judge. Marcellus confessed to disobeying the emperor and continued to proclaim his Christian faith. He was then sent before a strict military official for punishment. Marcellus reaffirmed his actions, and the Roman official sentenced him to death. The court secretary, Cassian, was so angered by the sentence that he refused to record it, and strongly denounced the injustice. He was imprisoned and eventually martyred himself, and is mentioned on December 3rd. Marcellus was taken out and beheaded, and his relics were eventually brought to León in Spain. He is thus patron of that city and province, as well as of conscientious objectors.

Also honored on this day are St. Serapion of Antioch; St. Germanus of Capua; St. Alphonsus Rodriguez; St. Tarkin; St. Asterius; St. Arilda; St. Angelo of Acri; and many other martyrs, confessors, and holy virgins.

text:
$TXT, $TYL, $AXGN, $GEN and $LHX. Five earnings calls, and some very interesting developments that I think deserve a closer look.

I spent some time going through these companies' latest earnings reports and management discussions.

And what caught my attention wasn't necessarily the revenue growth or the earnings beats.

It was what management revealed about the businesses themselves.

An aircraft manufacturer that cannot complete certain planes because of specialized components. A software company whose customers want to migrate to the cloud but cannot move quickly. A medical company expanding into new surgical procedures. A cybersecurity business becoming a financial services platform. And a defense manufacturer trying to expand an entire industrial supply chain.

These are the kinds of developments I look for when researching companies.

1. $TXT | Textron. Strong aircraft demand, but manufacturing remains the real challenge.
Textron owns businesses including Cessna, Beechcraft and Bell.

It manufactures business jets, turboprops, helicopters, military aircraft and defense systems.

One of the most interesting things from the earnings call was that aircraft demand is not the main problem.

Completing those aircraft efficiently is.

Textron delivered more Citation jets than a year ago, but Aviation profit increased much more slowly than revenue.

Why?

Because production is still being affected by shortages of specialized components, including engines, wing spars and auxiliary power units.

Think about what that means operationally.

An aircraft can be almost entirely assembled, with millions of dollars already invested in materials and labor, but it cannot be delivered because one critical component is unavailable.

The manufacturer continues carrying inventory, labor costs and production inefficiencies while waiting for the missing part.

And in aviation, you cannot simply replace a specialized component with something similar. Suppliers and parts must meet demanding certification and quality requirements.

Textron has qualified an additional wing spar supplier and is considering more internal manufacturing.

That could help, but bringing production in house also requires investment.

The second interesting development is Bell's MV-75 military aircraft program.

The aircraft is progressing technically, but its financial performance has been affected by government funding timing and changing contract cost estimates.

The Army has secured additional funding, yet some earlier charges have not been reversed. Management also expects a larger future program adjustment than previously anticipated.

This is why I don't treat every defense backlog as guaranteed profitable revenue.

One last detail caught my attention.

Textron raised its cash flow outlook, but management explained that much of the improvement comes from lower expected capital spending.

That is not the same as generating more recurring operating profit.

My read: Real aircraft demand and valuable defense programs, but the company still needs to prove that production efficiency and contract margins are improving.

I want to see more completed deliveries, better Aviation margins and stable MV-75 contract economics.

2. $TYL | Tyler Technologies. A software company with a very interesting customer problem.

Tyler develops software used by governments.
Courts, tax departments, public safety agencies, licensing offices and other public institutions rely on its systems to operate.

These are not applications that customers can casually replace.

A government might have years of records, employee training, integrations and public services built around Tyler's software.

Replacing that system can require significant time, money and administrative approval.

That creates strong customer relationships, but also makes growth complicated.

Tyler is moving customers from traditional installed software to cloud subscriptions.

Management has previously indicated that moving a customer to SaaS can generate approximately 1.7 times the annual revenue of the old maintenance arrangement.

That is interesting because the company doesn't necessarily need a completely new customer to grow.

It can generate more revenue from its existing customer base.

But there is a problem.

A government agency cannot always approve and complete a software migration quickly.

Contracts must be negotiated, budgets approved, data transferred, employees trained and systems tested.

That explains something unusual from the earnings call.

The annual value of new SaaS contracts increased much faster than reported SaaS bookings.

Part of the reason was shorter contract durations.

A customer signing a higher-value one-year agreement can contribute less total booking value than a customer signing a smaller annual agreement for three years.

So bookings alone can give an incomplete picture.

Another interesting development is Tyler's first multitenant enterprise ERP implementation.

The goal is to move customers toward a more standardized cloud architecture, reducing the complexity of maintaining numerous separate software installations.

If that works at scale, it could improve margins and make future upgrades easier.

And then there is AI.

Tyler already has approximately 300 deals containing AI functionality and is expanding its agentic software offerings.

But management acknowledged that meaningful incremental revenue from these newer products is unlikely before the second half of 2027.

My read: I like the recurring business model and the potential to increase revenue from existing customers.

But I want to see contracts turn into completed migrations and recognized revenue.

A signed deal is not the same as a fully operating system.

3. $AXGN | Axogen. This is probably one of the most unusual companies in this group.

Axogen develops products used to repair damaged peripheral nerves.

When a nerve is severed, surgeons sometimes need to bridge the gap between its two functioning ends.
Traditionally, that can involve removing a healthy nerve from another part of the patient's body.

That creates another surgical site and can cause complications.

Axogen's Avance product uses processed donor nerve tissue to provide a biological structure through which regenerating nerve fibers may grow.

The company has already established commercial sales and received FDA approval for Avance, although some indications remain subject to additional confirmatory evidence.

But the interesting part is where the business could go next.

Axogen recently acquired BioCircuit Technologies, the developer of NerveTape.

NerveTape is designed to help surgeons connect and protect nerve ends without conventional microsuturing.

That means Axogen can potentially address additional surgical procedures, including direct nerve repair where a separate graft is not required.

The commercial logic is straightforward.

Axogen already has relationships with surgeons and hospitals.

If it can introduce another useful product through those relationships, it may generate additional revenue without building an entirely separate sales organization.

But there is another development that deserves even more attention.

Axogen is exploring nerve reconstruction during prostate cancer surgery.

In some prostate procedures, nerves involved in sexual function cannot be preserved.

Axogen is investigating whether reconstruction using its technology can improve functional recovery in selected patients.

Management reported encouraging early clinical observations and plans to present more detailed findings on November 9.

This could become an interesting new application.

But I would be very careful here.

Early patient outcomes are not proof that the treatment itself caused the improvement.

We need appropriate comparison groups, patient selection data, longer follow-up and stronger clinical evidence.

And although the existing Avance business is growing, the recent acquisition required substantial equity financing.

That means existing shareholders must consider dilution alongside company growth.

My read: A real commercial nerve repair business with an interesting product expansion.

The prostate opportunity deserves research, but I would not treat it as proven revenue or established clinical efficacy.

Clinical evidence first. Commercial adoption second. Financial returns after that.

4. $GEN | Gen Digital. The company behind Norton and Avast is becoming something different.

Most people know Norton and Avast as cybersecurity products.

But Gen Digital is expanding beyond traditional antivirus software.

Its portfolio now includes identity protection, privacy products, MoneyLion and Engine.
And I find the business model increasingly interesting.

Gen effectively has two different economic engines.

The traditional Cyber Safety business provides device protection, identity monitoring and related subscriptions.

This business is mature and highly profitable.

The newer Trust-Based Solutions business includes financial wellness, consumer finance tools and marketplace services.

It is growing faster, but with lower operating margins.

That creates an important financial distinction.

A company can increase total operating profit while its consolidated margin percentage declines.

If a lower-margin business generates substantial additional revenue and profit, the company can become more valuable even though the average margin falls.

This is why I don't automatically classify every margin decline as evidence of deteriorating execution.

What matters is the incremental profit and the capital required to generate it.

The second interesting part is distribution.

Gen already has a large customer base and relationships with employers, telecommunications companies and other partners.

Instead of acquiring every new customer through advertising, it can offer additional products through those existing relationships.

For example, someone using Norton for cybersecurity might eventually access identity protection or financial wellness products within the same ecosystem.

Engine can also connect consumers with financial product providers.

But more customer engagement doesn't automatically mean more profitable revenue.

The company needs to demonstrate that product recommendations turn into completed transactions, subscriptions and attractive customer lifetime economics.

There is also an interesting application of AI inside the company.

Management reported that approximately half of customer support contacts are now resolved end to end using AI.

If that reduces support costs while maintaining service quality, it can improve profitability without requiring a major new revenue stream.

And that is different from launching an AI feature and hoping customers pay for it.

My read: A profitable cybersecurity business expanding into financial services through an established customer network.

I like the distribution opportunity, but the debt load, financial product economics and returns from acquisitions need close attention.

5. $LHX | L3Harris. The missile business is growing, but manufacturing capacity is the real story.

L3Harris develops military communications, electronic warfare systems, sensors, space technology and missile propulsion systems.

The latest earnings report included major multiyear contracts for THAAD and PAC-3 missile propulsion.

The company reported record backlog.

But the most interesting question is not how large those contracts are.
It is whether L3Harris can manufacture and deliver the required systems profitably.

Producing a solid rocket motor is not like assembling an ordinary industrial product.

It requires specialized materials, propellant manufacturing, precision components, testing, trained workers and strict quality controls.

Expanding production requires more than building another factory.

And management understands this.

L3Harris is investing heavily in missile manufacturing capacity, but approximately one quarter of that investment is directed toward suppliers.

Why?

Because expanding final assembly is useless if critical suppliers cannot deliver the necessary components.

The company is trying to increase capacity across the entire production chain.

That is a much more interesting strategy than simply announcing a larger factory.

Another detail from the earnings call caught my attention.

L3Harris reduced a rocket motor quality inspection process from approximately 21 hours to 6.5 hours through automation.

That is a major operational improvement for that specific process.

Faster inspection can increase throughput without requiring proportionally more inspection resources.

But it only creates sustainable value if the quality of the inspection remains reliable.

There was also an unusual supply chain issue.

Management said shortages of certain printed circuit board materials had affected revenue, partly because those materials were also in demand from other electronics applications.

It shows how production bottlenecks can emerge several layers below the final manufacturer.

Now for the financial side.

L3Harris raised its near-term earnings guidance, but reduced its 2028 free cash flow target from $3.5B to $3B.

Part of the reduction reflects a decision to fund employee retirement contributions with cash instead of issuing new shares.

That consumes cash but can reduce shareholder dilution.

The company is also accelerating manufacturing investments.

So the lower cash flow outlook is not automatically evidence of weaker demand.

But it does mean shareholders need to evaluate whether those investments eventually generate sufficient returns.

And one more distinction matters.

A substantial portion of L3Harris's contractual backlog remains unfunded.

That does not mean the orders are meaningless, but future cash generation depends on government appropriations, contract execution and actual deliveries.

My read: Strong demand and meaningful production expansion, but the investment case depends on manufacturing throughput, funded orders and future cash generation.

A large backlog is valuable only when it can be converted into profitable deliveries.

Now, what do these five earnings calls tell me?

I see five different business mechanisms, and five different questions that matter more than the headline earnings beat.

For $TXT, the question is whether aircraft orders can become completed deliveries without production inefficiencies destroying margins.

For $TYL, it is whether government software contracts can become operating cloud systems that generate higher recurring revenue.

For $AXGN, it is whether clinical evidence, surgeon adoption and new products can generate profitable growth without excessive dilution.

For $GEN, it is whether an established cybersecurity customer base can support a broader financial services business with attractive economics.

And for $LHX, it is whether military orders can become funded production, accepted deliveries and sustainable free cash flow.

What I find interesting is that all five already have some form of commercial evidence.

They are not simply companies presenting a theoretical market opportunity.

But the strength of that evidence is different in each case.

Some have established recurring revenue and cash generation.

Others depend more heavily on manufacturing execution, new product adoption, clinical validation or future funding.

And that is where I want to concentrate my research.

My next step is understanding what the market is already pricing into each company.

A good business can still be an unattractive investment at the wrong valuation.

And a promising earnings development doesn't automatically make the chart a good entry.

I still want to examine the financials in more detail, compare them with the valuations, and review the weekly and daily charts before deciding which companies deserve closer monitoring.

My final read.

The most interesting information in an earnings call is often not the earnings number itself.

It is the explanation of why the company is growing, what is limiting that growth, and what management must accomplish next.

That is where I believe we can find useful information before it becomes obvious in the financial statements.

Not a buy list. Just five businesses with developments worth investigating.

Business reality first. Financial evidence second. Valuation and chart confirmation before capital.

My investing journal, not financial advice.
